items.fix: Gate it: 50–60% scroll depth, or 30+ seconds, or exit intent. Persist the dismissal and do not show it again for at least 30 days. Never stack it over a consent banner, and never show it on checkout or on a page a visitor reached from search with a specific intent.
items.before: useEffect(()=>setShowModal(true),[])
items.after: show on scrollDepth > 0.6 && !localStorage.getItem('nl-dismissed'), then record the dismissal on close
items.false_positive_when: Age gates, jurisdiction gates and consent banners legally required on first paint. Onboarding dialogues inside an authenticated app after signup. A/B-tested variants where immediate display was a measured decision.

items.name: cost-revealed-at-last-step
items.description: The price shown on the product page and in the cart excludes shipping, service fees or mandatory taxes, which first appear on the final checkout screen after the address and card have been entered.
items.detection: Crawl product → cart → checkout. Flag when the first DOM occurrence of /shipping|delivery|postage|tax|VAT|service fee|handling|booking fee/i alongside a monetary value happens only on the final step, and the displayed total changes between the penultimate and final step. Static proxy: a cart summary rendering only subtotal where the order model carries shipping and tax fields.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The generated cart computes what it can compute locally — line items — and defers anything needing an address or a rate table. The result is textbook drip pricing produced by arithmetic convenience rather than intent, landing precisely on the UK DMCC Act's total-price requirement, in force since April 2025.
items.fix: Show a shipping estimate on the product page (or a clear "free over X"), and expose the full breakdown in the cart before checkout begins. Where the exact figure needs a destination, show a range and the threshold.
items.before: Cart: Total £49.00  →  Checkout step 3: Total £57.95
items.after: Cart: Subtotal £49.00 · Shipping from £3.95 · Estimated total £52.95, with a postcode estimator
items.false_positive_when: Taxes that genuinely cannot be computed before a destination is known — the requirement is disclosure of their existence and basis, not a precise figure. B2B checkouts quoting ex-VAT to VAT-registered buyers as the market convention. Genuinely optional add-ons are outside the mandatory-fee rule.

items.name: docs-generator-defaults-unmodified
items.description: The docs site is a create-docusaurus, Mintlify or Nextra starter with the content swapped and nothing else: scaffold primary colour, scaffold logo and favicon, scaffold footer columns, scaffold sidebar labels, and the generator's own name still in the footer.
items.detection: Docusaurus: src/css/custom.css still carrying the scaffold green --ifm-color-primary: #2e8555 and its six generated shades; static/img/logo.svg or favicon.ico byte-identical to the template; docusaurus.config footer.links still Docs/Community/More with Stack Overflow, Discord and X entries; tagline still "Dinosaurs are cool"; docs/intro.md still present. Mintlify: starter colors.primary and the starter Quickstart/Development nav intact. Flag at min_markers co-occurring markers.
items.why_it_reads_ai: "Set up a docs site" resolves to running the scaffolder, and the scaffolder's output is already a complete, good-looking site — so the loop terminates. The tell is not ugliness; it is that the site is indistinguishable from the starter, which the Docusaurus team themselves called out: "the sample sites above use different colors, but still look quite the same".
items.fix: Change four things at minimum: the primary colour token set, the logo and favicon, the footer link groups, and the landing page. Delete every scaffold page — intro.md, tutorial-basics/, the blog with Welcome and MDX Blog Post.
items.before: --ifm-color-primary:#2e8555; + the Docusaurus dinosaur logo + footer Stack Overflow / Discord / X
items.after: brand token set, real logo and favicon, footer linking to the repo, status page, changelog and support
items.false_positive_when: A day-one docs site where shipping content matters more than theming — real and defensible. Teams deliberately standardising on an unmodified theme to cut maintenance. Internal docs where branding is pointless. One marker alone is never enough.

items.name: sidebar-nested-past-three-levels
items.description: A left sidebar with four or more levels of collapsible nesting, so finding a page requires guessing three parent categories correctly, and the whole tree is collapsed on arrival.
items.detection: Parse the sidebar config — Docusaurus sidebars.js category nesting, Mintlify navigation groups, Nextra _meta.json, MkDocs nav — and flag maximum depth at or beyond max_depth. Corroborating: most leaf pages sitting at depth three or deeper.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Deep nesting is what you get when a category is created for every noun rather than for a reader's task. Generators mirror the source-file tree, which is organised for authors.
items.fix: Three levels maximum: section → group → page. Flatten by merging categories with fewer than three children. Expand the current section by default. Make the top level answer "what am I trying to do", not "what module is this".
items.before: API → Reference → Resources → Users → Methods → createUser
items.after: API reference → Users → createUser
items.false_positive_when: Very large reference corpora — cloud provider APIs, standards documents — where depth reflects the domain and search carries the load. Auto-generated SDK references mirroring namespaces, navigated by search rather than browsing.

items.name: docs-search-indexes-nothing
items.description: The docs site has a search box in the navbar and no index behind it — either no search plugin is configured at all, or the Algolia block still contains placeholder credentials.
items.detection: A docs site whose theme renders a search UI where none of docusaurus-search-local, docusaurus-lunr-search, theme-search-algolia (with real appId/apiKey/indexName), pagefind or typesense is configured; OR an algolia config containing YOUR_APP_ID, YOUR_SEARCH_API_KEY, YOUR_INDEX_NAME or an xxx placeholder. Rendered: search a string from the current page's h1 and get zero results.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Same family as decorative-site-search, and specific to docs because the theme ships the search UI whether or not you supply an index — so the generator gets a search box for free and never discovers it is hollow. Search is the primary navigation mode for docs; a hollow one is worse than none.
items.fix: Wire a local index — docusaurus-search-local or Pagefind: no external service, works offline, indexes at build. Apply for DocSearch only if you want hosted. Then search for a string you know exists and confirm.
items.before: algolia: { appId: 'YOUR_APP_ID', apiKey: 'YOUR_SEARCH_API_KEY', indexName: 'YOUR_INDEX_NAME' }
items.after: themes: [['@easyops-cn/docusaurus-search-local', { hashed: true, indexBlog: false }]]
items.false_positive_when: Search wired through a platform feature invisible to a repo scan — Mintlify, GitBook and ReadMe index server-side. Sites under about fifteen pages where the sidebar is the whole IA and search was deliberately removed. Search delegated to a parent-domain site search.

items.name: no-version-selector
items.description: Documentation for software that has shipped breaking changes, with only the current version published and no way to read the docs for the version the reader is actually running.
items.detection: The project's published latest version is 2.0.0 or higher (or the repo has two or more major tags), and the docs build has no versioning: no versions.json or versioned_docs/, no mike config, no version dropdown in the navbar config, no /v1/ route.
items.why_it_reads_ai: UNREVIEWED, and genuinely contested. Versioning is an ongoing maintenance commitment and experienced maintainers argue both sides — which is why this is low. The narrow, uncontested case is: breaking changes shipped, old majors still supported, no way to read their docs.
items.fix: Cut a version snapshot at each major. If you will not, say so prominently, keep a changelog with migration notes, and make sure every page states which version it describes.
items.before: one docs tree; the reader is on v1 and every example is v3
items.after: a version dropdown — v3 (current) / v2 / v1 — or a banner naming the version these docs describe
items.false_positive_when: Projects with strong backward compatibility where one tree is honestly correct — Redis's maintainer makes exactly this argument. Hosted SaaS with no user-visible versions. Pre-1.0 projects. Products where a changelog plus per-page "since v2.3" annotations do the job.

items.name: code-sample-not-runnable
items.description: Code blocks the reader cannot use: no language tag, elisions like "// ... rest of your code", unexplained <YOUR_API_KEY>, shell blocks with a leading $ on every line that the copy button then copies, and no complete example anywhere.
items.detection: Across .md and .mdx: fenced blocks with an empty info string as a share of all blocks; blocks containing /\.\.\.|\/\/ ?(rest of|your code here|implementation|etc)/; shell blocks where most lines start with $; placeholders /<(YOUR|MY)_[A-Z_]+>|YOUR_API_KEY|xxxx+/ with no adjacent instruction on where to obtain the value; and no block in the page set that is a complete runnable file.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model writes illustrative fragments because fragments are what documentation prose looks like in the corpus; it never pastes one into a terminal. The $-prefix case is a specific, nasty one — it LOOKS like a terminal transcript and silently breaks paste.
items.fix: Tag every fence with a language. Strip $ prompts from copyable shell blocks. Ship at least one complete, copy-paste-and-run example per page, and run it in CI so it cannot rot.
items.before:
```
$ npm install foo
$ foo init --key <YOUR_API_KEY>
```
items.after:
```bash
npm install foo
foo init --key "$FOO_API_KEY"
```  — plus a line saying where FOO_API_KEY comes from
items.false_positive_when: Conceptual documentation where a fragment is the point. Output blocks — a terminal transcript deliberately showing prompt and response — which correctly include $ and are not meant to be copied. Blocks tagged text or console on purpose.

items.name: every-page-opens-with-in-this-guide
items.description: Page after page opens with the same throat-clearing: "In this guide, we will…", "By the end of this article, you'll…", "Let's dive in." The reader scrolls past a paragraph of table-of-contents-in-prose on every page.
items.detection: Share of docs pages whose first body sentence (after the H1 and frontmatter) matches /^(in this (guide|article|tutorial|section|post|chapter)|this (guide|article|tutorial|document) (will|covers|explains|walks)|by the end of this|let'?s (dive|get started|take a look)|we'?ll (walk|cover|explore|take a look))/i. Flag at page_share of pages, or min_consecutive consecutive pages. The uniformity is the signal; one instance is not.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A human writing twenty pages varies the opening, because writing the same sentence twenty times is unbearable. A generator writing twenty pages independently produces the highest-probability opening twenty times.
items.fix: Delete the opening paragraph and start with the first real sentence. If the page needs orientation, state the outcome in one line and let the H1 and the sidebar TOC do the structural work.
items.before: In this guide, we will walk through the process of configuring authentication. By the end of this article, you'll have a working setup. Let's dive in.
items.after: Configure SSO with Okta in about ten minutes. You need admin access to both accounts.
items.false_positive_when: Long-form tutorials where one framing paragraph genuinely orients the reader — the tell is repetition across pages, never a single instance. House styles mandating a "What you'll learn" block, which should then be a structured component rather than prose. Translated docs where the construction is idiomatic in the source language.

items.name: api-reference-restates-the-type
items.description: Generated reference where every description is the identifier re-spelled in English: "userId: string — The user ID." No units, no ranges, no defaults, no errors, no relationship to any other field.
items.detection: Judge primarily. Static heuristic: for each documented parameter, split the identifier on camel and snake boundaries and compare with the description; flag when token overlap is at or above overlap after stopword removal, or the description matches /^(The|A|An) <identifier words>\.?$/i, or is five tokens or fewer. Flag a PAGE when most of its entries qualify.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Mixed, and worth stating plainly: this is the oldest failure in technical writing, now cheaper to mass-produce. TypeDoc, JSDoc and godoc have emitted this shape for twenty years; a model asked to document a set of types produces it at scale and at speed. Read it as UNREVIEWED-at-volume rather than distinctively machine-written.
items.fix: For each parameter add at least one thing the signature does not contain: unit, range, default, what happens when it is omitted, what it interacts with, or an example value. If you cannot add anything, delete the description — an empty one is more honest than a tautological one.
items.before: timeout: number — "The timeout."
items.after: timeout: number — "Milliseconds to wait for a response before aborting. Default 30000. Values under 1000 are clamped. Aborting raises TimeoutError, which is retryable."
items.false_positive_when: Genuinely self-describing fields in a large uniform schema, where boilerplate would add noise. Reference pages that exist to be searched and are paired with real prose guides elsewhere — reference is MEANT to be terse. Machine-readable specs consumed by tooling rather than read.

items.name: no-real-product-photography
items.description: Every product has exactly one image, all images share a single stock host or a single generated aesthetic, and there are no alternate angles, no scale reference, no variant-specific photos and no user-submitted images.
items.detection: Flag when: median images per product is one; all product image hosts resolve to one stock CDN or one generation pipeline; filenames follow product-\d+\.(jpg|png|webp); variant selectors exist but do not change the image; no zoom, lightbox or gallery component in the build. Judge on the set: do these images share one lighting setup and one background such that they cannot be photographs of different real objects?
items.why_it_reads_ai: A different measurement from the image-forensics tells: this is about COVERAGE, not pixels. A real catalogue accumulates photographic inconsistency — different days, different lights, a hand in one shot. Perfect visual uniformity across a catalogue is the tell, and it is exactly what a generated store produces.
items.fix: Photograph the actual product from at least three angles plus one in-use or scale shot. If you are reselling, use supplier imagery and say so. Make variant selection change the image. Never present a generated image as a photograph of a physical good.
items.before: one stock-CDN image per SKU, identical studio background across unrelated categories
items.after: 4–6 real images per SKU including scale and detail; a variant-linked gallery
items.false_positive_when: Digital goods, services and software — there is nothing to photograph. Pre-launch catalogues with placeholder imagery tracked on a checklist. Brands with a deliberate, disclosed 3D-render pipeline, which is legitimate when the render is accurate and labelled. Marketplaces early in seller onboarding.

items.name: spec-table-as-prose
items.description: Dimensions, materials, compatibility and sizing written as a paragraph instead of a table the reader can scan or compare.
items.detection: A section whose heading matches /specification|specs|dimensions|size (guide|chart)|materials|technical details|what'?s included/i rendered as paragraphs or a bullet list rather than a table or definition list, containing min_pairs or more extractable label–value or number–unit pairs. Also flag a multi-column spec table, which readers misread as a comparison sheet, and a size chart rendered as an image.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generators write prose by default; a table requires deciding the schema. The prose reads fluently and destroys the one thing the reader came for, which is comparison. Baymard finds half of sites get spec-sheet scannability wrong.
items.fix: One-column table or definition list, grouped into semantic sections, with labels consistent across every product in the category so cross-product comparison works. Size charts as real tables with both metric and imperial, not as a JPEG.
items.before: Measures 42cm wide by 30cm deep by 18cm tall, made from powder-coated steel…
items.after: a table with rows: Width 42 cm / Depth 30 cm / Height 18 cm / Material powder-coated steel, oak veneer / Max load 25 kg
items.false_positive_when: Products with genuinely few specs, where a two-row table is worse than a sentence. Narrative product descriptions that accompany a real spec table elsewhere on the page. Apparel where fit is described qualitatively alongside a real measurements table.

items.name: checkout-without-guest-option
items.description: Checkout requires an account. The visitor with a full cart hits a login wall and a "create password" field before they can give you money.
items.detection: The checkout route is behind auth — middleware matcher including /checkout, or an if (!session) redirect('/login') in the checkout loader or handler — with no guest branch, no guestCheckout flag and no email-only path. Rendered: load the cart in a fresh session and attempt checkout.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Auth-gating a route is the default generated pattern for anything involving an order record, and guest checkout is an explicit exception someone has to ask for. The model optimises for a clean data model; Baymard measures the cost at roughly a fifth to a quarter of buyers.
items.fix: Email-only guest checkout as the default path, with account creation offered AFTER the order is placed and pre-filled from it. If you need an account for order history, create it silently and send a set-password link with the receipt.
items.before: /checkout in the auth middleware matcher, no exception
items.after: a guest path collecting email and address; post-purchase "Create an account to track this order" with the fields already filled
items.false_positive_when: Subscriptions, licensed software, regulated goods and B2B portals where an account is structurally required. Marketplaces needing buyer identity for dispute handling. Digital goods delivered to an account. Re-order flows for existing customers.

items.name: reviews-without-filtering-or-distribution
items.description: A star average and a list of review cards, with no rating histogram, no filter by star or attribute, no sort, no verified-purchase marker, and no way to find the one-star reviews — which is what the reader came for.
items.detection: A reviews component rendering an average plus items, with none of: a distribution bar chart per star value, a filter control, a sort control, or a verified field on the review model. Corroborating: every displayed rating is four or five stars while the claimed average is 4.9.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The average and the card list are the visible parts; the filtering apparatus is what makes reviews USABLE and is invisible in a screenshot. This is the apparatus, not the text — synthetic-review-shape covers fabricated review copy, and the two co-occur often enough to be worth checking together.
items.fix: Ship the histogram — it is the single highest-value element, telling the reader the shape of opinion in one glance — plus filter-by-star, sort by recency and helpfulness, and a verified-purchase badge that means something. Show the negative reviews; hiding them is what makes the positive ones unbelievable.
items.before: ★★★★★ 4.9 (127 reviews) + six 5-star cards
items.after: average + a 5→1 distribution bar chart + star filter + sort + verified badges
items.false_positive_when: Products with under about ten reviews, where filtering is pointless and the full list fits. Reviews delegated to an embedded third-party widget that provides the controls inside an iframe a static scan cannot see. B2B where reviews are curated case studies, clearly labelled as such.

items.name: email-built-with-web-css
items.description: The HTML email is built like a web page — display:flex, CSS grid, div columns, padding on div and p, a style block rather than inline styles, border-radius, position — and collapses in Outlook's Word rendering engine.
items.detection: On the template: display:flex or display:grid; position:absolute or fixed; float layout; max-width on a structural div with no mso conditional fallback; padding on div or p used for layout; a stylesheet link or a style block carrying layout rules with no inliner in the pipeline (juice, premailer, mjml, maizzle); layout tables without role="presentation"; no mso- conditional block anywhere.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The corpus of HTML is overwhelmingly WEB HTML; email HTML is a tiny, weird dialect frozen around 2003. The model writes the majority dialect. It renders perfectly in the preview pane the author checks and breaks in the client a third of recipients use.
items.fix: Use MJML or Maizzle and let them emit the table soup and the MSO conditionals. If hand-writing: nested tables with role="presentation" for layout, padding on td only, every style inlined, ghost tables for Outlook, mso conditionals for anything with a corner radius or a background image. Then test in a rendering service, not in Gmail alone.
items.before: …
items.after: ……
items.false_positive_when: Internal tools and dev-only notifications where the audience's client is known. Plain-text-style emails with minimal markup, which are MORE robust, not less. Teams that have measured their audience and confirmed no Word-engine Outlook.
items.evidence: Microsoft has said it will end Word-engine desktop Outlook support in October 2026, so this decays — slowly, and not at all for enterprise fleets on frozen builds.

items.name: no-plain-text-part
items.description: The send call supplies html only. No text/plain alternative, so text-only clients, accessibility tooling, smart-watch previews and several spam filters get nothing or an auto-generated mangle.
items.detection: Find the send call — resend.emails.send, sgMail.send, transporter.sendMail, ses.sendEmail, postmark.sendEmail, mailgun.messages.create — and flag any invocation whose options object sets html (or Body.Html) with no text, Body.Text or TextPart sibling in the same call.
items.why_it_reads_ai: html: is the documented minimum in every provider's quickstart, so it is what gets generated; the multipart alternative is the step the quickstart omits.
items.fix: Always send both parts, and write the text version deliberately — do not let the ESP auto-strip tags, which produces link soup. Keep the same links and the same unsubscribe.
items.before: await resend.emails.send({ from, to, subject, html })
items.after: await resend.emails.send({ from, to, subject, html, text })
items.false_positive_when: Templates managed inside an ESP where the text part is authored in the ESP UI rather than in code. Providers that genuinely generate a good text part, where the team has verified it. Transactional sends to a known machine consumer.

items.name: email-unreadable-with-images-off
items.description: The headline, the offer, the price and the CTA are all inside images. With images blocked — the default in several clients and common in corporate environments — the email is a stack of empty boxes.
items.detection: Compute the live-text-to-image ratio on the rendered template and flag when the only rendering of the primary heading or the primary CTA is an img or a background-image. Corroborating: images with missing or empty alt in a marketing template; a CTA implemented as an image with no text fallback and no bulletproof-button table.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Compounds with text-baked-into-image: the same instinct in a harsher medium, because email clients block images by default far more often than browsers do.
items.fix: Live text for every heading, price and CTA. Bulletproof buttons — a td with a background colour, padding and an anchor — rather than button images. Meaningful alt on every informative image, empty alt on decoration. Then preview with images disabled; it should still sell.
items.before: a single 600x900 hero-offer.png containing the entire email
items.after: live h1, live price, a bulletproof button td; images carry atmosphere only, all with alt
items.false_positive_when: Purely visual sends where the image IS the product — a photographer's portfolio drop, an art print announcement — which still need alt text and a text CTA, but where the ratio flag is the wrong instrument. Emails where a single decorative header image sits above substantial live text.

items.name: preheader-never-set
items.description: No preheader was authored, so the inbox preview shows whatever text comes first in the HTML — "View this email in your browser", an unsubscribe line, or a mailing address. Prime inbox real estate spent on boilerplate.
items.detection: The template's body does not begin with a hidden preheader element — canonically a div or span with display:none, font-size:1px, max-height:0, overflow:hidden, mso-hide:all, usually followed by zero-width-non-joiner padding. Flag when that element is absent AND the first visible text node matches /view (this )?(email|message) (in|on)|having trouble|can'?t see this|unsubscribe|update your preferences/i. Also flag a preheader that is a verbatim copy of the subject line.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The preheader is invisible in every preview the author looks at — it exists only in the inbox list view — so nothing in the loop surfaces its absence.
items.fix: First child of body: a hidden div with 40–100 characters that CONTINUE the subject rather than repeating it, followed by zero-width padding so no boilerplate leaks in behind it. Move "View in browser" below the preheader or into the footer.
items.before: …View this email in your browser → inbox shows "View this email in your browser"
items.after: Your October invoice is ready — £248.00, due 14 Nov.
items.false_positive_when: Plain-text or text-first emails whose first line is already good preview copy — that IS the preheader. Transactional sends where the opening line is deliberately the most important sentence. ESPs that inject the preheader at send time from a campaign field invisible to a template scan.

items.name: dark-mode-inverts-the-logo-away
items.description: A dark, transparent-background logo on a #ffffff email body. The client inverts the background to near-black, the logo does not invert, and the brand mark disappears — or a dark-mode override turns the whole template into an unreadable mid-grey.
items.detection: A logo img with a transparent-background PNG or SVG whose dominant ink is dark, where the template has none of: a prefers-color-scheme dark block, [data-ogsc] or [data-ogsb] selectors, a color-scheme plus supported-color-schemes meta pair, an mso conditional locking colours, or a light plate baked behind the mark. Corroborating: background-color:#ffffff on the outer table, which Outlook inverts most aggressively.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Dark mode in email is client-specific, partially undocumented and impossible to observe without opening the message in each client. It is the most "you had to be there" defect in this lane.
items.fix: Give the logo a baked-in light plate or outline so it survives either ground. Ship a dark variant via prefers-color-scheme where supported, with [data-ogsc] overrides for Outlook.com. Declare color-scheme and supported-color-schemes. Avoid pure #ffffff — #f7f7f7 inverts more gracefully. Then open it in Outlook Windows, Apple Mail and Gmail iOS in dark mode.
items.before: on bgcolor="#ffffff", no color-scheme metadata
items.after: logo with a light plate + color-scheme meta + a prefers-color-scheme block + [data-ogsc] overrides
items.false_positive_when: Logos already light-on-transparent, which survive inversion. Templates that are dark-first by design. Audiences on clients with no forced inversion. Teams that have consciously accepted the trade-off after testing.

items.name: unsubscribe-absent-or-buried
items.description: A bulk or marketing send with no List-Unsubscribe header, or no in-body unsubscribe link, or one rendered at 8px in the same colour as the background under three paragraphs of legal text.
items.detection: For any send classified as bulk or marketing: headers set with no List-Unsubscribe AND no List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click; no body anchor matching /unsubscribe|opt[- ]out|manage (your )?preferences/i; that anchor styled below min_font_px or at a contrast under 3:1 against its background; or the unsubscribe URL routing to a login page.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Headers are a layer above the template that nothing in a visual loop touches, and provider quickstarts do not include them. Since June 2024 this is a deliverability failure as much as a legal one — Gmail and Yahoo made one-click unsubscribe a condition of bulk delivery.
items.fix: Set both headers, honour the POST within two days, and keep a plainly visible in-body link in normal body colour at normal size. Never require a login to unsubscribe. Keep the link live at least 30 days after the send.
items.before: resend.emails.send({from,to,subject,html}) with a 9px grey "unsubscribe" in a legal block
items.after: headers: { 'List-Unsubscribe': '<https://…/u/{token}>, <mailto:unsub@…>', 'List-Unsubscribe-Post': 'List-Unsubscribe=One-Click' } plus a normal-weight footer link
items.false_positive_when: Genuinely transactional mail — receipts, password resets, security alerts, order status — which is exempt and should NOT carry one. Double-opt-in confirmations. Internal or system mail. The boundary is the message's purpose, not its list.

items.name: no-print-stylesheet
items.description: The page prints as a fixed header, a hamburger button, a cookie banner and three blank sheets, with link destinations invisible and content broken mid-element. Nobody ever pressed Ctrl-P.
items.detection: No @media print rule anywhere and no <link media="print">. Aggravating signals in the same build: position:fixed or sticky on header or nav; height:100vh or min-h-screen sections; overflow:hidden on a scroll container holding content; dark backgrounds with light text; no break-inside:avoid on cards, tables or figures. Severity rises to high where the page is an invoice, receipt, ticket, itinerary or legal document. Rendered: print to PDF at A4 and count blank pages.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Print is not in the generation loop at all — the least-visited surface in this lane. It is also among the cheapest to fix: a twelve-line @media print block covers most of it.
items.fix: Add a print block that hides chrome, unpins fixed positioning, resets viewport-height sections, avoids breaking inside headings, tables and figures, prints link destinations after external anchors, and sets a page margin. Then actually print it.
items.before: no print rules; page 1 is the nav, pages 2–4 are blank
items.after: @media print { header, nav, footer, [role="dialog"] { display:none !important } * { position:static !important } h2, table, figure { break-inside:avoid } a[href^="http"]::after { content:" (" attr(href) ")" } @page { margin:15mm } }
items.false_positive_when: Web applications and dashboards with no sensible print form, where a dedicated export is the right answer. Sites shipping a "Download PDF" or print-specific route a CSS scan will not see. Pages inside a print-aware framework such as Paged.js. Purely interactive experiences.

items.name: receipt-generated-as-screenshot
items.description: The invoice, receipt, ticket or report PDF is a rasterised screenshot of a web page. No selectable text, no search, no copyable amount or reference number, unreadable to a screen reader, and two megabytes.
items.detection: In any invoice, receipt or export code path, a rasterising call — page.screenshot(, html2canvas(, domtoimage., sharp(…).png() feeding a PDF writer, or jsPDF.addImage( with a canvas source — instead of page.pdf( or a PDF library (pdfkit, pdfmake, react-pdf, wkhtmltopdf, weasyprint). Artifact check: the produced PDF has no /Font objects, or pdftotext returns empty, or each page is a single image XObject.
items.why_it_reads_ai: "Generate a PDF of this page" retrieves a Puppeteer snippet, and screenshot() is the more prominent method. The output looks right in a viewer and is functionally dead — it cannot be pasted into accounting software, searched for an invoice number, or read aloud.
items.fix: page.pdf({format:'A4', printBackground:true}) — Chromium's PDF output preserves real text AND honours your print stylesheet, so this and no-print-stylesheet are fixed by the same work. For structured documents, generate the PDF from data with a PDF library and tag it so amounts and totals are machine-readable.
items.before: const png = await page.screenshot(); doc.addImage(png,'PNG',0,0,w,h);
items.after: const pdf = await page.pdf({ format:'A4', printBackground:true, margin:{top:'15mm'} });
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate image exports — an OG card, a share graphic, a chart thumbnail — that were never meant to be documents. Snapshot and visual-regression test paths. Systems where a rasterised, watermarked artefact is a deliberate anti-tamper decision.

items.name: fingerprint-is-not-authorship
items.description: The governing rule for every fingerprint in this lane, and the one most often broken. A generator meta, a CDN host or a scaffold dependency tells you WHAT MADE the page. It does not tell you who wrote it, and it does not tell you whether the page is any good.
items.detection: Not a check. A posture applied to every other item in this lane: report the platform if asked, never infer the author, and never report a provenance string as a quality finding.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Three collapses to refuse. Provenance is not authorship: lovable-tagger in a repo proves a project STARTED in Lovable and says nothing about six months of commits since. Provenance is not defect: server: Pepyaka and framerusercontent.com are infrastructure, and deleting them is either impossible or pointless. And absence proves nothing: every badge in this lane is removable by paying, so "no badge" is not evidence of hand-building. The sharpest case is Wix and Squarespace, whose AI flows now seed the ordinary editor — their AI-built and hand-built output is provably identical in markup, so any finding of the form "this is AI-generated because it is on Wix" is false.
items.fix: When a pure provenance string is all you have, say one line: this page is served by X, that is information rather than a problem, decide whether you want it visible. Then move on to the craft findings, which are where the value is.
items.before: "This site was AI-generated — it has a Framer generator meta."
items.after: "This site is published from Framer. That is a design tool used by professional teams and by Framer's own AI agent, and the markup is identical either way. Separately, here are six things about the page that are worth fixing."
items.false_positive_when: There is no false positive on the strings themselves — they are exact literals. The false positive is always in the inference drawn from them.

items.name: fix-what-the-fingerprint-points-at
items.description: The overlap set, and the reason this lane earns its place: a handful of fingerprints are ALSO defects, where the provenance string and the craft problem are the same bytes. These are the only ones worth editing, and the fix is never to hide the string.
items.detection: The set: content="Generated by v0" (provenance AND no meta description); og:image at bolt.new/static/og_default.png (provenance AND every share posts the builder's logo); Lovable's R2 screenshot og:image (provenance AND the share card was never authored); <meta name="keywords" content="keyword"> (provenance AND a shipped placeholder); href="/vite.svg" (provenance AND the favicon is a build tool's logo); shadcn's exact default oklch tokens (provenance AND nobody chose the palette); Framer's per-glyph spans (provenance AND screen readers hear "W e   B u i l d"); Gemini_Generated_Image_*.png as an author headshot (provenance AND a person who does not exist).
items.why_it_reads_ai: In each case the string survived because the surface it sits on is one nobody looks at during a chat-driven build: the browser tab, the share card, the meta description, the chart palette. The preview pane shows none of them.
items.fix: Fix the thing the fingerprint points at, never the fingerprint. Write the description. Make the OG image. Choose the palette. Replace the headshot with a real one. The string disappears as a side effect, which is the only removal that is honest — an audit that says "strip the generator meta" is teaching concealment, and it will not survive contact with someone who has to defend the site to their boss.
items.before: "Remove the v0 generator tag before launch."
items.after: "Your meta description is the string 'Generated by v0', so search results and every shared link describe the tool instead of the product. Here is a 155-character description."
items.false_positive_when: None. This item is a routing rule, not a detector.

items.name: agent-instruction-shipped-to-production
items.description: A comment addressed to a language model, left in the artifact a visitor downloads. Lovable ships one telling the model not to delete a script tag; Replit ships one explaining a dev-only banner to a reader who was never supposed to exist.
items.detection: Exact literals, both verified at scale by code search: the Lovable comment "IMPORTANT: DO NOT REMOVE THIS SCRIPT TAG OR THIS VERY COMMENT!" next to https://cdn.gpteng.co/gptengineer.js (36,032 hits), and the Replit comment "This is a replit script which adds a banner on the top of the page when opened in development mode outside the replit environment" next to replit.com/public/js/replit-dev-banner.js (7,296 hits in HTML files). Either half alone is sufficient.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nothing announces machine authorship more plainly than a literal instruction to a machine, shipped. This is the residue family in its purest form: near-zero human source, because no person writes a comment addressed to a model and then publishes it.
items.fix: Delete the comment and the script from the production template. For Replit's dev banner this is also a real fix — it is a third-party script on every pageview of a live site. For Lovable's, confirm the editor still works first.
items.before: <!-- IMPORTANT: DO NOT REMOVE THIS SCRIPT TAG OR THIS VERY COMMENT! -->
items.after: neither the comment nor the script in the shipped HTML
items.false_positive_when: Prompt-collection and documentation repositories carry these strings as their subject matter, not as a site. Filter to HTML actually served from an origin.

items.name: scaffold-title-and-favicon-residue
items.description: The scaffold's own title, favicon, description and share image shipped to production. A law firm with the Vite logo in the browser tab; a business whose social card is the builder's own logo.
items.detection: Exact literals: <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/vite.svg"> and <title>Vite + React</title>; <title>Create Next App</title> and content="Generated by create next app"; <title>v0 App</title>, content="Generated by v0", content="Created with v0"; <title>React App</title> and a stray %PUBLIC_URL%; og:image at bolt.new/static/og_default.png. Also worth flagging: a <title> that restates the build prompt rather than naming a brand — "Trading Mitra Financial Website", "AI-Powered CRM Dashboard".
items.why_it_reads_ai: The favicon and the share card are the two most-seen bytes of any site and the two nobody looks at during a chat-driven build, because the preview pane renders neither. The title that restates the prompt is the same failure one level up: the page is named after the request that produced it.
items.fix: Four lines: a real title, a real meta description, a real favicon, and a real og:image on your own domain. Verify against the DEPLOYED HTML rather than the builder's preview — on v0 the metadata change appears only in the deployed project.
items.before: <title>v0 App</title> + <meta name="description" content="Generated by v0"> + href="/vite.svg"
items.after: <title>Prolific Pours — mobile bartending in NYC</title> + a description saying what the page is for + the brand mark as favicon + a 1200x630 card on the site's own domain
items.false_positive_when: Genuine scaffolds, starter repos, boilerplate and tutorial demos, where "Create Next App" is the honest title of the thing. Filter to sites with a custom domain or real business content.

items.name: builder-default-og-image
items.description: The Open Graph image is the builder's property rather than the site's: Bolt's own logo, or a Cloudflare-hosted screenshot of a Lovable preview build. Every share of the business's site posts somebody else's picture.
items.detection: content="https://bolt.new/static/og_default.png" on og:image or twitter:image. And Lovable's auto-screenshot, matched as pub-[0-9a-f]{32}\.r2\.dev/[0-9a-f]{32}/id-preview-[0-9a-f-]+\.lovable\.app-\d{13}\.png — which is the most durable fingerprint in this lane, because it survives badge removal AND a custom domain.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The share card is invisible in every preview the builder shows, so nothing in the loop surfaces it. In the Lovable case it is worse than a default: the card was auto-generated by screenshotting a preview environment, so every link posts a robot's snapshot of an unfinished build.
items.fix: Ship a real 1200x630 og:image on your own domain. One change fixes the share card and removes the fingerprint, which is the right order to do it in.
items.before: <meta property="og:image" content="https://bolt.new/static/og_default.png">
items.after: <meta property="og:image" content="https://yourdomain.com/og.png">
items.false_positive_when: None for the string. A deliberate demo or a tutorial page may honestly carry the builder's card.

items.name: shadcn-default-tokens-untouched
items.description: The mechanism behind "every AI site is the same purple", and it is measurable as exact constants. shadcn/ui's default theme ships specific oklch values; finding them unmodified proves the palette was never chosen.
items.detection: Grep the shipped CSS for the literal defaults: --radius: 0.625rem; oklch(0.769 0.188 70.08) (--chart-5); oklch(0.828 0.189 84.429) (--chart-4); oklch(0.398 0.07 227.392) (--chart-3); oklch(0.6 0.118 184.704) (--chart-2); --sidebar-ring: oklch(0.708 0 0). Any one of the chart values is a near-unique literal; code search returns 164,352 files carrying the block byte-identical.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The tokens are identical across thousands of sites because nobody replaced them. Note that swapping the hue does not change the system — practitioners report newer models reaching for orange instead of violet, with the same gradient and the same card, which is the point: the palette is a default whichever colour it defaults to.
items.fix: Replace the whole token block with real brand values — including --chart-* and --sidebar-*, which are the ones people forget. Changing only --primary leaves five default chart colours that appear the first time anyone renders a graph.
items.before: --chart-5: oklch(0.769 0.188 70.08);  in a fintech dashboard's production CSS
items.after: a five-value brand chart ramp, contrast-checked against the surface it draws on
items.false_positive_when: Using shadcn/ui is not a defect — it is a mainstream, well-engineered library used by large teams. The finding is UNMODIFIED DEFAULTS, never the library's presence. A project that renders no charts may reasonably leave the chart tokens alone; check whether they are used before reporting.

items.name: ai-image-default-filenames
items.description: Image generators assign distinctive default download filenames and site builders preserve them, so the filename in the img src names the model that made the picture. Midjourney's format contains the prompt.
items.detection: Grep src, srcset and content attributes for: Gemini_Generated_Image_ (and WordPress's derived cropped-Gemini_Generated_Image); the concatenated ChatGPT form ChatGPTImage<Mon><DD><YYYY><HH>_<MM>_<SS><AM|PM>.png and the hyphenated WordPress-sanitised ChatGPT-Image-Oct-20-2025-11_57_34-AM; Midjourney's <discorduser>_<prompt_words_underscored>_<uuid>.png; and, weakly, a UUID-only filename where every other asset is descriptively named.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The strongest content-provenance signal available, and it survives every rebuild, migration and badge removal, because the filename travels with the file. It has already been used in published investigative reporting to establish that author headshots on a network of sites were generated, alongside credentials the named university confirmed never existed.
items.fix: Rename every image to a descriptive slug before upload — worth doing on search grounds regardless. But if the image is a person or a proof artifact, renaming is the wrong fix: replace it, or remove it.
items.after: a real photograph at /team/marta-oleszek.jpg, or no photo at all
items.false_positive_when: Generated imagery is routine and legitimate for illustration and background art. The finding is AI imagery used WHERE A HUMAN OR A PROOF IS IMPLIED — bylines, team pages, testimonials, client work. And a descriptive filename proves nothing in the other direction: absence of this tell is not evidence the image is real.

items.name: per-character-text-spans
items.description: Per-character text animation emits one span per glyph, often with an inline colour on each. The result is visually fine and semantically shredded: screen readers, copy-paste, text extraction and search engines all see letter-spaced garbage.
items.detection: Strip tags from the body and look for runs of isolated single characters — (?:(?:^|\s)\S(?=\s)){6,}. On a live Framer template this extracted as "W e   B u i l d   B r a n d s". Confirm by finding adjacent single-character spans in the markup.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It reads effect-first: the animation was chosen before the content was considered, which is the hallmark of a page assembled from motion presets rather than written. Note this is a DEFECT fingerprint rather than a TOOL fingerprint — GSAP SplitText, Webflow text-split interactions and several React libraries produce the same shape, so pair it with a generator string before naming a tool.
items.fix: Turn per-character animation off for anything that is real page copy — headings, value propositions, body. Reserve it for decorative marquees, and give those aria-hidden with a plain-text sibling. If it must stay on an H1, add a visually hidden un-split copy of the same string.
items.before: We B…
items.after: the heading is one text node; the animation runs on a wrapping element, not on split children
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate typographic art where the letters are the content, and elements already marked aria-hidden with a readable sibling.
items.evidence: Corrects a widely repeated claim. A heavily upvoted r/TechSEO comment holds that Framer "essentially create SPAs like Gmail or Netflix uses — there is only an empty div in the body". That is false: a Framer template page was measured at 11,126 characters of server-rendered visible text and 51 headings in the body. The real problem is narrower and more interesting, and it is this one.

items.name: keywords-meta-placeholder
items.description: A meta keywords tag — an element search engines have ignored since 2009 — shipped with the literal placeholder value "keyword", or stuffed with a comma-salad of service-plus-location phrases that are four restatements of one idea.
items.detection: <meta name="keywords" content="keyword"> is the unmistakable form, verified live on a production business site. The generated form looks like "bartending service NYC, bartender for hire NYC, private bartending NY, mobile bar NYC" — flag the repetition, not the tag.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The keyword list is a fossil of the generation prompt. Repetition without variation is the same pattern that shows up in the visible body copy, which is why this tag is worth reading even though it does nothing.
items.fix: Delete the tag. Then check whether the visible section headings are that same list in sentence form; if they are, rewrite to one specific claim per section.
items.before: <meta name="keywords" content="keyword"/>
items.after: tag removed; each section makes one claim the others do not
items.false_positive_when: Many content management systems still emit a keywords tag from an SEO plugin. The literal value "keyword" is the part with no innocent explanation.

items.name: unclaimed-default-subdomain
items.description: A commercial site whose only address is the builder's auto-assigned subdomain. In v0's case the URL publishes the prompt: v0-ai-powered-crm-for-dentists.vercel.app tells a visitor exactly what was typed to make their vendor's website.
items.detection: The address itself: *.lovable.app, *.bolt.host (including raw 25-character base36 ids), *.base44.app, v0-<prompt-slug>.vercel.app, *.framer.website/.media/.app, *.replit.app, durable.site, and Hostinger's <css-colour-name>-<animal>-<6 digits>.hostingersite.com.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nobody decided the address; the builder assigned it. It is the cheapest credibility problem to describe and the cheapest to fix.
items.fix: Buy the domain. For v0 specifically, rename the project too — the slug is a louder tell than any meta tag, because it is a transcription of the prompt.
items.before: a law firm's contact page at eqovo83f889a4stmo1auvr4u9.bolt.host
items.after: firmname.com
items.false_positive_when: Prototypes, internal tools, hackathon entries, demos and staging URLs all legitimately live on default subdomains. Only a finding when the page is transacting or soliciting.

items.name: single-file-cdn-tailwind-page
items.description: The shape a chat surface produces, because a chat surface can only hand you one file: everything inlined, Tailwind loaded from the Play CDN, React from a UMD build with Babel in the browser, no build artifacts, no favicon. Recorded here as an honest negative result — ChatGPT Canvas leaves NO provenance marker at all, and this catalog will not invent one.
items.detection: By shape, not by string: <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"> (which Tailwind documents as not for production) plus one style block, one script block, no /_next/ and no hashed asset bundle, plus a missing or emoji-data-URI favicon.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It does not, reliably, and that is the point of the entry. The Play CDN in production is a genuine performance defect — an uncached third-party script that must run before first paint and generates CSS at runtime — and that is the finding worth making. The authorship inference is not available and should not be attempted.
items.fix: Run a real Tailwind build and ship a compiled stylesheet. If the page is genuinely one-file-by-design, at minimum pin a versioned CDN build and inline the critical CSS.
items.before: <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script> in a production head
items.after: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.<hash>.css"> from a real build
items.false_positive_when: Frequently. Prototypes, internal tools, teaching examples, single-page microsites and pen-style demos legitimately use the Play CDN, and plenty of people write single-file HTML on purpose. This is the weakest entry in the lane and should be scored lowest; never assert authorship from it.

items.name: supabase-anon-surface-unprotected
items.description: The default data layer of several builders is Supabase called straight from the browser with an anon key, and scaffold-created tables land with Row Level Security disabled unless somebody turns it on.
items.detection: In network traffic or the bundle: a <ref>.supabase.co/rest/v1/ origin with an apikey header carrying a JWT. Then TEST it — issue an unauthenticated GET /rest/v1/<table>?select=* with the public anon key from an incognito session. The finding is the response, not the architecture.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The scaffold cannot infer who should see which rows, so it ships the permissive default and the human never revisits it. One scan of a builder's own showcase found 10.3% of apps with critical RLS failures exposing names, addresses, phone numbers and financial records; a wider scan of 1,072 vibe-coded apps found 98% with security issues and 16% critical.
items.fix: Enable RLS on every table and write explicit policies. Verify with the anon key from an incognito session, not by reading the dashboard.
items.before: GET /rest/v1/leads?select=* with the public anon key returns every customer record
items.after: the same request returns []; authenticated requests return only the caller's rows
items.false_positive_when: The presence of Supabase calls is normal architecture and not a defect. Only an actual unauthenticated read of private data is a finding — do not report "uses Supabase" as a security issue, test it.

items.name: status-code-only-file-probe
items.description: A methodology warning, recorded because implementing the naive version makes an audit wrong in public. Probing for leaked agent files by HTTP status alone returns a false positive on every single-page-app host, because they serve index.html for all unknown paths.
items.detection: Measured directly: /CLAUDE.md, /AGENTS.md, /.cursorrules, /.env and /package.json ALL returned HTTP 200 on live Bolt and Base44 sites, and all of them returned the site's index.html. The rule: a probe counts only if the content-type is not text/html AND the body does not begin with <!DOCTYPE or <html AND the body parses as the expected format. In the sample, exactly one probe survived that test and it was a real package.json.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A genuinely exposed CLAUDE.md or .cursorrules at the web root is both a strong provenance signal and a real information leak, so it is worth checking — correctly.
items.fix: For the site owner: make sure the build output excludes agent config and the host does not serve repository files. For anyone auditing: implement the content check before shipping the probe.
items.before: GET /.env → 200 → "the environment file is exposed"
items.after: GET /.env → 200, content-type text/html, body starts <!DOCTYPE → not a finding
items.false_positive_when: By default, on every Vite or Next single-page host. Never ship a status-code-only probe.

items.name: client-first-class-system
items.description: A negative finding, included because suppressing a false positive is worth as much as raising a true one. Finsweet's Client-First is a human naming convention for Webflow. Generated output does not produce it and neither do code generators, so finding it is positive evidence of a human starting point.
items.detection: Class literals: padding-global, container-large/medium/small, padding-section-small/medium/large, max-width-large, spacer-*, text-size-*, and components named in the section_hero / hero_component form.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It does not — that is the entire point. Use it to lower confidence in other signals on the same page.
items.fix: Nothing to fix. Record it and weigh the other findings accordingly.
items.before: hashed one-off class names throughout
items.after: padding-global, container-large, section_hero — a system somebody chose and applied
items.false_positive_when: Client-First can be applied to a bought template that was barely touched, so it evidences that a human system was used, not that a human designed this site. And a Client-First site can still have machine-written copy — this signal covers markup provenance only.

items.name: template-versus-generated
items.description: The disambiguation rule between "somebody bought a starting point" and "a model wrote this". It matters because a template is a human choosing a starting point — often a good decision — and misreporting it as generation destroys trust in the whole audit.
items.detection: Template signals: a theme name or author credit in the markup; systematic class naming (Client-First, BEM, a theme prefix) rather than hashed one-offs; demo-content residue (Lorem ipsum, John Doe, Your Company Name, "Blog post title"); and feature surplus — a pricing table, a team grid, a blog and a shop on a site that needs none of them, because templates include everything. Generated signals: hashed one-off class names, no theme header, no demo residue but heavy invented specificity — named fake clients, invented metrics — and exactly the sections that were asked for and no more.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Neither, necessarily. The useful contrast is that templates ship DEMO content and generators ship PLAUSIBLE INVENTED content. Lorem ipsum is a template; a fabricated testimonial from a named person at a named company is not.
items.fix: Report as "this appears to be template X, lightly customised" if you can name it. Otherwise say nothing about provenance and review the craft.
items.before: "AI-generated — it looks like every other agency site."
items.after: "This is a marketplace template with the demo content still in three sections. Those sections are the finding."
items.false_positive_when: The two categories overlap heavily now: AI builders ship template libraries and template marketplaces ship AI-assisted templates, so the sameness predates the generators and is partly a marketplace effect.

items.name: case-study-process-without-artifacts
items.description: A portfolio case study that narrates a process and shows nothing from it. Discovery, personas, a double-diamond diagram, a journey map — then a hero mockup and a metric with no source.
items.detection: For each case study, ask: does it contain at least one artifact that could only exist if the work happened — a screenshot of the shipped product, a before-and-after of a specific screen, a sketch in somebody's handwriting, a redline, a rejected direction? If the only images are a device mockup of the final screen plus generic diagrams, flag it. Supporting static tells: stock sticky-note-wall imagery, a double-diamond SVG, a journey map shaped like a zoomed-out spreadsheet, and percentage claims with no methodology.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Process language is the easiest thing in the world to generate and the hardest thing to fake evidence for. A model can write "we synthesised insights across 14 stakeholder interviews"; it cannot produce the interview notes. In a portfolio this is not a detail — it is the whole product.
items.fix: Add one artifact per case study that could not have been generated: a photo of the whiteboard, the actual design file, the rejected direction and one sentence on why it lost, a screenshot of the dashboard behind the metric. One real artifact beats three paragraphs of process.
items.before: "Through extensive user research and iterative prototyping, I identified key pain points… Result: conversion increased 34%."
items.after: "We shipped the one-field checkout in March. Here is the funnel before and after [screenshot]. 34% is the completed-checkout rate over six weeks; the sample is 11,200 sessions."
items.false_positive_when: Work under NDA genuinely cannot show artifacts — but the honest version is a one-line statement of the constraint plus a redacted artifact, not generic process prose. Junior and student portfolios legitimately foreground process because that is what they have; do not review one the way you would review a senior portfolio.

items.name: selected-works-of-three-and-third-person-about
items.description: The exact skeleton portfolio generators emit, published in their own marketing: a Selected Works grid of exactly three projects, an About written in the third person about a first-person subject, and a "Let's work together" close.
items.detection: A heading matching /^(Selected Works?|Featured Work|Recent Work)$/i directly above a grid of exactly three cards; a heading matching /Let'?s (work together|build something|create something|talk)/i; and an About section whose first sentence uses the subject's own name in the third person while the rest of the page says "I". The person mismatch is the sharpest of the three.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Three is the generator's default cardinality, not a curatorial decision, and the vendors say so outright — one advertises producing "case-study pages, a selected-work gallery, an about section, and contact" from a short description of your discipline. That is the skeleton, named by the people selling it.
items.fix: Show a number of projects that is not three — two if you have two good ones, seven if you do; the number should look like a decision. Pick one grammatical person and hold it. Replace "Let's work together" with what you actually want.
items.before: "Selected Works" / three cards / "Maya is a multidisciplinary designer based in Lisbon." / "Let's work together."
items.after: "Four projects I'd defend" / four cards / "I'm Maya. I design onboarding for fintech, mostly." / "I have one project slot open in March — here is what a good fit looks like."
items.false_positive_when: Three genuinely good projects is a normal and defensible edit, and many excellent portfolios show exactly three. Third-person About is a real convention for agencies and for people who get press-quoted. Flag only when both appear together, or when the person shifts within the page.

items.name: invented-clients-and-generated-bylines
items.description: The one place in this whole catalog where a finding is about honesty rather than craft: a "Trusted by" wall, a testimonial, a team grid or an author byline where the entities cannot be verified and the supporting image is generated.
items.detection: Run the AI-image filename check against every image inside a testimonial, team, author or client section. Check whether logo-wall marks are all the same optical weight and grid aligned (generated) or varied (real). Then for each named client or person, look for off-site corroboration: a link, a case study on the client's own site, a profile, a press mention. Cross-check testimonials attributed only to a first name and a job title, and "as featured in" with no links.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generators fill proof slots with plausible content because the slot exists in the template. The template asked for six client logos, so six client logos appeared. Published reporting has already found this in the wild: generated author headshots, profiles all created within days of each other, and claimed Oxford degrees the university confirmed never existed.
items.fix: Delete every unverifiable claim. An empty "Trusted by" section is better than a fabricated one. Replace with what is true and checkable — one named client with a link, or a plain statement of how long you have been doing this and for whom.
items.before: six logo marks of companies with no relationship to the business; a team page of four generated headshots
items.after: one real client with a linked case study; a photograph of the actual person, or no photograph
items.false_positive_when: Concept and spec work is legitimate in a portfolio — the defect is UNLABELLED concept work presented as client work. A stock or illustrated avatar is fine if it does not claim to be a person. And logo walls sometimes honestly show tools used rather than clients: read the heading before you read the logos.

items.name: agency-proof-gap
items.description: An agency or freelancer site that claims capability its own build contradicts. The pitch and the page were written by the same process, so neither checked the other.
items.detection: The contradiction test, run against the site's own artifacts: "we build high-performance websites" on a page shipping 127 font files; "custom design, no templates" on a page with an unmodified shadcn chart token; "we refuse to be boring" on a violet-gradient glass-card hero; "bespoke" on a builder subdomain with a build tool's favicon. Static support: any builder badge on a site selling web services, and the builder's default share card.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is the one finding that costs money directly, and it is the clearest case of the generation loop having no outside reader. Every claim is plausible in isolation; the page itself is the counter-evidence.
items.fix: In order: fix the contradiction the site makes about itself before touching the copy — remove the badge, set the share card, buy the domain. Then replace every unevidenced superlative with one checkable fact. If you build with these tools, say so as a positioning choice rather than hiding it badly.
items.before: "Award-winning digital studio crafting bespoke experiences" — on a builder subdomain, with the builder's logo as the share card
items.after: "We build marketing sites in about a week. Three recent ones, with what each cost and what it does now: [links]."
items.false_positive_when: Using a builder for your own agency site is a defensible efficiency decision and many good agencies do it openly. The finding is the GAP between claim and artifact, never the tool. Small agencies legitimately have few public case studies early on, and "no proof yet" is a different thing from "invented proof".

items.name: builder-lockin-and-export-illusion
items.description: The recurring complaint after the fact is not "it looks bad" but "I cannot leave, and the export is not what I thought". Worth naming because it is a real cost of the category that the sales page does not mention.
items.detection: Readable from the fingerprints: a site whose content lives inside a platform context object or a hydration payload has no portable content layer, and there is no export that reconstructs the design. Practitioners put it plainly — once you export and touch the code, you usually lose the visual editor workflow completely.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Not a machine tell at all. It is the structural cost of hosted builders, and a skill that reviews these sites should be able to name it honestly rather than only critiquing the pixels.
items.fix: Advice rather than a code change. Before committing, verify three things: can you export content as structured data, can you export or self-host the rendered site, and what happens to your URLs. Several major platforms fail the second. The durable arrangement is content in a portable store with the builder as a rendering layer.
items.before: three years of content on a hosted builder, and moving means a full rebuild
items.after: content authored in markdown or a headless store; the builder renders it
items.false_positive_when: Lock-in is a legitimate trade for speed. For a site that will be replaced in eighteen months anyway it costs nothing. Only a finding where longevity matters.

items.name: design-pattern-is-not-provenance
items.description: How much to trust the public "is this AI" detectors, and which half of their method to steal. The string layer is sound; the aesthetic layer is not.
items.detection: The credible layer is generator metas, script paths, CDN hosts, known CNAMEs and HTTP headers — the same signals technology-profiling tools have used for a decade, with near-zero false positives. The layer to refuse is the aesthetic one: "purple-to-blue gradients, shadcn components, Lucide icons, glassmorphism cards, sparkle emoji in headings, a recently registered domain" describes thousands of well-made hand-built sites, and domain age is not evidence of authorship at all.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the failure mode this entire skill is built to avoid, appearing in tools that claim to do what this skill refuses to do. Naming it here keeps the boundary visible.
items.fix: Two things worth adopting. Detect in a rendered DOM, because attributes like the Lovable tagger's only exist after hydration. And band your confidence: three or more signals in the same category is a positive, two is probable, one is a hint and usually not enough. Weight the fingerprint strings and the design patterns at different tiers and never let the second promote the first.
items.before: "Purple gradient plus Inter plus rounded cards, therefore AI."
items.after: "Three Tier-A strings put this on Lovable. Separately, the palette is unmodified, which is a craft finding whoever built it."
items.false_positive_when: Any detector scoring aesthetics as authorship evidence will misfire on a large fraction of good 2024–2026 product sites. Report tool provenance from strings, report craft from craft, and never infer one from the other.

items.name: automation-covers-a-third-of-this
items.description: The frame for this whole lane, and the reason it exists. The most generous number any vendor publishes is Deque's own: axe-core surfaces 57.38% of issues BY VOLUME — high precisely because the things automation catches (missing alt, low contrast, unlabelled fields) are the most numerous. Measured by distinct success criteria a machine can fully verify, coverage is about 30%, roughly 15 of WCAG 2.1 AA's 50. Everything in this file sits in the other 70%.
items.detection: Not a check. A routing rule: a green automated scan is the START of an accessibility review, never the end, and a report that consists of a passing axe run has established almost nothing. Where an item here is marked assistive, a headless browser cannot settle it — the finding is what a person HEARS.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Mostly UNREVIEWED rather than machine-written. A hand-built 2011 jQuery site fails most of this too. What IS distinctively model-flavoured is a smaller set, and it has one shape: the model produces the APPEARANCE of accessibility work. An aria-label on a div, a redundant role on a semantic element, a role promised with no behaviour behind it, a live region that is conditionally rendered and therefore silent, alt text that describes the photograph instead of doing its job, and an accessibility statement asserting a conformance level nobody measured. Those six are the ones to weight.
items.fix: Run the automated pass, then do the five-minute manual pass in references/five-minute-manual-pass.md, which is written for someone who has never used a screen reader. It finds the majority of what this lane covers and every step of it passes axe.
items.before: "Accessibility: axe reports 0 violations."
items.after: "axe reports 0 violations, which covers about a third of the criteria. Eleven minutes of keyboard and screen-reader testing found six things it structurally cannot see."
items.false_positive_when: None — this is a framing item, not a detector. Note the number cuts both ways: automated tooling is genuinely valuable for the numerous, mechanical failures, and skipping it because it is incomplete would be worse.
items.evidence: From the disability community's side of the same fact, on the Overlay Fact Sheet: "There are 0 automated tools that can detect accessibility problems accurately at anything above 30% of the time." And the correlation that makes the cargo-culted-ARIA entries defensible rather than aesthetic — WebAIM Million 2026: home pages WITH ARIA averaged 59.1 errors against 42 for pages without, and "the more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility errors could be expected". ARIA use rose 27% in a year to 133 attributes per page. Correlation, not cause — but it is a 17-error penalty attached to exactly the behaviour a model performs when asked to make something accessible.

items.name: focus-order-diverges-from-reading-order
items.description: Tab order does not follow the order things are read. Two causes, and only one is greppable: a positive tabindex, or — far more common in generated code — CSS that visually reorders content while DOM order stays as written.
items.detection: Static for the cheap half: any positive tabindex; and order:, flex-direction:*-reverse or grid placement on containers holding interactive children. Rendered for the half that matters: walk the DOM in source order, compare against the sequence Tab actually produces, and flag any pair whose focus order inverts their on-screen top-then-left order by more than one position. axe flags positive tabindex and stops; it has no concept of visual order.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Unreviewed. A model asked for "the image on the right on desktop and above the text on mobile" reaches for order-1 lg:order-2, because that is the framework idiom, and nobody Tabs the result. The tell is not the CSS; it is that no person ever pressed Tab.
items.fix: Change the DOM order and delete the order utility. Where a visual swap is genuinely needed at one breakpoint, keep the interactive elements in reading order and reorder the non-interactive wrappers around them. Never use tabindex above 0 — W3C's F44 names it as a documented failure of 2.4.3.
items.before: — the submit button is reached before the label text explaining it
items.after: , with the arrangement handled by source order
items.false_positive_when: order on presentational wrappers containing no focusable children is harmless. A single deliberate swap between two prose columns is fine. Positive tabindex inside a third-party embed is not your finding. And a rendered check dispatching synthetic Tab produces garbage inside roving-tabindex composites — exclude anything within role=grid, toolbar, tablist or tree.

items.name: spa-route-change-focus-lost
items.description: Client-side navigation swaps the view; focus stays on the link that was clicked or is dumped to the body, the document title does not change, and nothing is announced. To a screen reader user the page did not navigate — it went quiet.
items.detection: Rendered: focus a nav link, press Enter, read document.activeElement; flag body, html, or the originating link. Snapshot document.title before and after and flag if unchanged. Static pre-filter only: a router import with zero .focus() calls and no title-setting anywhere in the route components. No automated engine can see this — axe scans one DOM snapshot and a route change is just a different snapshot.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Unreviewed, and a framework gap rather than a model one — client-side routing has had this hole since 2014. It earns its place because generated apps are overwhelmingly SPAs by default, so the BASE RATE in generated work is near total while hand-built work at least sometimes noticed.
items.fix: In ONE layout-level component, not scattered per route: on route change set document.title, then move focus to the new view's h1 carrying tabindex="-1". Do not announce AND move focus — moving focus to a heading makes the screen reader read it, which is the announcement.
items.before: a route element with no focus or title handling anywhere in the tree
items.after: a route announcer in the layout that sets document.title and focuses the main heading on pathname change
items.false_positive_when: Frameworks that already do this — check for the built-in before filing. Modal-like and drawer routes legitimately keep focus where it is. A "route change" that only updates a query param and filters a list in place should NOT move focus; that is the silent-results finding instead.

items.name: focus-never-enters-the-dialog
items.description: A modal opens visually and focus stays behind it on the trigger, so Tab then walks the page UNDERNEATH the overlay. Distinct from escape-and-focus-declared-not-wired, which is declared behaviour failing at runtime; this is behaviour that was never declared.
items.detection: Rendered: open by keyboard and assert the dialog contains document.activeElement. Then Tab past the focusable count inside and assert focus never lands outside the dialog.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Model-flavoured enough to say so, on a clean panel design: across roughly three thousand driven trials, 24% of generated modals put focus inside on a bare prompt, rising to 66% with explicit guidance; only 12% fully held focus, rising to 64% guided. Per-model leak rates on bare prompts ran from 7% to 33%.
items.fix: Native <dialog> opened with showModal(), which does this for free, or a maintained primitive. If hand-rolled must stay, focus the first meaningful control on open — not the dialog container.
items.before: a conditionally rendered overlay with role="dialog" and no effect that focuses anything
items.after: <dialog ref={ref}> opened with ref.current.showModal()
items.false_positive_when: Non-modal dialogs and popovers deliberately leave focus alone until the user Tabs in. A dialog opened programmatically without user action — a session-expiry warning — may correctly not steal focus mid-typing, though it must then announce. Stacked dialogs move focus to the topmost layer on purpose.

items.name: focus-not-restored-on-dismiss
items.description: The dialog, drawer, menu or command palette closes and focus is dropped to the body. The keyboard user is teleported to the top of the page and has to Tab back. Sighted keyboard users describe this as the most disorienting bug in modern web apps, and it is invisible in a screenshot.
items.detection: Rendered: record document.activeElement before opening; close by EACH available route — Escape, the close button, a backdrop click — and assert focus returned to the recorded element every time. Generated code frequently restores on the button and not on Escape.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Unreviewed. The open path gets tested because you can see it work; the close path does not, because visually nothing is wrong.
items.fix: APG is explicit: focus returns to the invoking element unless that element no longer exists, in which case it goes somewhere that provides logical workflow. Native <dialog> restores automatically. If the trigger was destroyed by the action, focus the nearest surviving sibling or the container heading — never nothing.
items.before: const close = () => setOpen(false)
items.after: const close = () => { setOpen(false); triggerRef.current?.focus(); } — with a fallback for when the trigger is gone
items.false_positive_when: When closing completes a flow that moves the user elsewhere on purpose. A create-item modal that closes and focuses the newly created row is BETTER than restoring to the trigger. Do not flag intentional forward motion.

items.name: focus-lands-on-the-container-not-a-control
items.description: Focus is moved on open — to the dialog div itself, or a wrapper carrying tabindex="-1" — rather than to the first control. The screen reader reads the dialog's name and the user is then standing on a non-interactive box. It looks correct in code review and passes an activeElement assertion, which is exactly why it survives.
items.detection: Rendered pre-filter: document.activeElement after open matches a dialog role or has tabindex="-1" with no widget role. Assistive to settle: open with a screen reader running and listen — you should hear the dialog name and THEN a control, not the name followed by the whole body read as one block.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Unreviewed, and specifically over-corrected: this is the shape of a fix applied from a half-remembered rule ("move focus to the dialog") without the second half of it.
