sources.title: Reinhart et al., 'Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles', PNAS 122 e2422455122 (2025)
sources.note: 8,290 parallel human/LLM texts over a 66-feature Biber tagset. Present participial clauses at 5.3x the human rate (d=1.38) is the top-ranked discriminating feature; nominalizations at 2.1x. The authors explicitly refuse the detector framing and argue for 'teachable moments in the revision of machine-generated text' — which is this skill's whole posture.

sources.title: Kobak, Gonzalez-Marquez, Horvat & Lause, 'Delving into LLM-assisted writing through excess vocabulary', Science Advances (2025)
sources.note: 15M+ PubMed abstracts. 'Delves' excess ratio 28.0; at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts LLM-processed. The methodological finding matters more than the word list: pre-2024 excess words were 79% nouns (content), 2024 excess words 66% verbs (style).

sources.title: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, 'GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers', Patterns 4(7):100779 (2023)
sources.note: Seven detectors, 61.3% mean false-positive rate on TOEFL essays; 19% flagged by all seven unanimously. Prompting for more native-sounding word choice dropped misclassification from 61.3% to 11.6% — proving the detectors measure fluency, not machine-ness.

sources.title: Weber-Wulff et al., 'Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text', International Journal for Educational Integrity 19:26 (2023)
sources.note: 14 tools, 756 tests. No tool exceeded 80% accuracy; GPTZero produced a 50% false-accusation rate on human text. Accuracy falls to ~45% on lightly human-edited AI text, so the detectors miss the machines and catch the people.

sources.title: van Nuenen, 'Voice Under Revision: LLMs and the Normalization of Personal Narrative', arXiv:2604.22142 (2026)
sources.note: The best study of what LLM EDITING does, with 13 markers and effect sizes: dashes +325.7%, commas +66.6%, contractions -31.4%, first-person pronouns -8.6%, lexical diversity +52.7%. Voice-preserving prompts recover only 10-15% of what is removed.

sources.title: Abdulhai et al., 'How LLMs Distort Our Written Language', arXiv:2603.18161 (2026)
sources.note: Adjectives +40-87% even under explicit minimal-edit prompts; pronouns -40-61%; a 68.9% increase in essays that take no position. Human-editor baseline is under 5% change in any POS category.

sources.title: Hart, Allred, Abbas & Alugo, 'The Deontic Gap', arXiv:2608.18144 (2026)
sources.note: Eleven-model replication. Personal deontic modals (should, have to, can't) sit at the 3.7th percentile of underuse — more underused than 96% of common vocabulary, so not a generic frequency artifact.

sources.title: Munoz-Ortiz, Gomez-Rodriguez & Vilares, 'Contrasting linguistic patterns in human and LLM-generated news text', Artificial Intelligence Review 57:267 (2024)
sources.note: The peer-reviewed basis for the sentence-length claim: human texts have more scattered length distributions, models cluster at 10-30 tokens, all differences p<0.001. Cite this rather than 'burstiness', which is a detection product's marketing vocabulary, not a term of art.

sources.title: Vanderbilt University, 'Guidance on AI detection and why we're disabling Turnitin's AI detector' (2023)
sources.note: The institutional arithmetic: a claimed 1% false-positive rate across 75,000 papers is 750 wrongly accused students. Northwestern, Michigan State and UT Austin followed.

sources.title: OpenAI, 'New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text' (retired 20 July 2023)
sources.note: Withdrawn six months after launch 'due to its low rate of accuracy'. At launch it caught 26% of AI text and falsely flagged 9% of human text.

sources.title: Simon Willison, 'Delve' (2024), summarizing Alex Hern's Guardian TechScape
sources.note: The fairness problem at the root of the best-known tell: 'delve' is markedly more common in Nigerian formal English, and the RLHF annotation workforce that rewarded it was substantially Nigerian and Kenyan. A list that flags 'delve' is mechanically a list that flags a dialect.

sources.title: GIJN, 'Reporter's Guide to Detecting AI-Generated Content'
sources.note: Why the hands-and-text image heuristic is retired, and what replaced it: provenance first — C2PA/Content Credentials, EXIF, reverse image search, publisher sourcing.

sources.title: grain — anti-slop linter for AI-assisted codebases
sources.note: A shipping deterministic linter whose rule list is effectively a pre-validated catalog: OBVIOUS_COMMENT, NAKED_EXCEPT, RESTATED_DOCSTRING, VAGUE_TODO, SINGLE_IMPL_ABC, HEDGE_WORD, THANKS_OPENER, BULLET_PROSE, VAGUE_COMMIT.

sources.title: melissawm/open-source-ai-contribution-policies
sources.note: Survey of project AI policies. Roughly forty REQUIRE disclosure, which is why stripping an agent-attribution trailer is a policy decision to check rather than a cleanup to perform.

sources.title: WebAIM Million 2026 — annual accessibility analysis of the top 1,000,000 home pages
sources.note: The external anchor for the web-defect lane, and the industry naming the cause itself: 95.9% of home pages fail WCAG, 56.1 errors per page, up from 51, 'reversing a trend of gradual accessibility improvements' — attributed to 'increased reliance on 3rd party frameworks and libraries and automated or AI-assisted coding practices (vibe coding)'.

sources.title: Why AI-generated websites all look the same - parix.ai
sources.note: The causal arrow that unifies the landing-page taste lane: 'An underspecified prompt gets answered with the statistical average of every landing page on the internet... Ask a model to design a landing page without giving it real content and it will invent placeholder copy - and placeholder copy produces placeholder layout.'

sources.title: Pull quote - Wikipedia
sources.note: The definition that makes pull-quote provenance checkable: 'a key phrase, quotation, or excerpt that has been PULLED from an article and used as a page layout graphic element.' A pull quote that appears nowhere else in its document is not a pull quote.

sources.title: Block Quotes and Pull Quotes: Examples and Good Practices - Smashing Magazine
sources.note: Draws the line the detector implements: pull quotes are excerpts of the presented text, while block quotations refer to an external citation not already in the article. Also the density guidance: an ordinary article should carry at most one or two.

sources.title: ELI-Why: benchmarking the pedagogical utility of LLM explanations (arXiv:2506.14200)
sources.note: The evidence that breaks the tidy unification of the exposition family. 13.4K why-questions and two human studies: GPT-4 explanations match their intended educational background only 50% of the time against 79% for lay human-curated ones, and explanations generated across model families for different informational needs remain indistinguishable in grade level. Prompting the audience does not fix altitude lock.

sources.title: Know Your Audience: do LLMs adapt to different age and education levels? (arXiv:2312.02065)
sources.note: Corroborates the same finding independently: current LLMs have set readability ranges and do not adapt well to different audiences even when prompted.

sources.title: The Curse of Knowledge: Pinker Describes a Key Cause of Bad Writing - APS
sources.note: The human mechanism the context-leakage family is the machine analogue of: 'It simply doesn't occur to the writer that readers haven't learned their jargon, don't seem to know the intermediate steps that seem to them to be too obvious to mention.' Underlying literature: Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber 1989; Nickerson 1999.

sources.title: Featherstone, AI UI accessibility: operability under browser-driven testing
sources.note: The evidence behind the declared-but-not-wired signature, and the best numbers in the whole catalog: ~3,000 browser-driven trials across a six-model panel. Escape handlers present in 79% of generated modals and working in 59%; 1,031 of 1,032 failures threw NO console error; focus fully held in 12% of bare prompts. Also the counterintuitive finding that asking for accessibility can reduce basic function.

sources.title: Featherstone, AI UI accessibility: the markup baseline
sources.note: 720 trials. 673 generated modals hand-rolled role=dialog on a div; about 2% used native <dialog>, essentially all from one model family. Native dialogs closed on Escape 98% of the time against 31% for hand-rolled ones.

sources.title: A11yN and the systematic review of LLM-generated accessibility
sources.note: LLMs replicate accessibility flaws from their training data rather than inventing new ones, which is why the fix is changing what they reach for (native elements, maintained primitives) rather than prompting harder.

sources.title: NN/g: Flat vs. deep website hierarchies
sources.note: Flat vs deep IA as a researched trade-off with costs on both sides. The finding the skill draws on is not that either is better — it is that generated navigation reflects no choice at all, which is a third thing.

sources.title: NN/g: Menu design — 15 UX guidelines
sources.note: "Failing to indicate the current location is probably the single most common mistake we see on website menus."

sources.title: NN/g: Hamburger menus and hidden navigation hurt UX metrics
sources.note: "Discoverability is cut almost in half by hiding a website's main navigation." Task time is longer and perceived difficulty rises; the desktop case is worse than the mobile one.

sources.title: NN/g: The 10 most violated homepage guidelines
sources.note: "Don't include an active link to the homepage on the homepage" — 41% compliance, tenth most violated.

sources.title: NN/g: Breadcrumbs — 11 design guidelines
sources.note: Including the guideline not to use breadcrumbs where no hierarchy exists — which is exactly where generated ones appear.

sources.title: NN/g: Duplicate links on a page
sources.note: Duplicate links "increase the number of choices users must make and generate unnecessary cognitive strain", with the picture-plus-label exception that makes a naive duplicate check noisy.

sources.title: W3C i18n: Personal names around the world
sources.note: "You should ask yourself whether you really need to have separate fields for given name and family name"; avoid the labels first name and last name. Stronger than "support more formats".

sources.title: WCAG 3.1.2 Understanding: Language of Parts
sources.note: Without correct language marking, assistive technologies do not switch pronunciation rules or voice packs. The basis for treating a frozen lang attribute as a defect rather than a nit.

sources.title: WCAG 1.4.5 Understanding: Images of Text
sources.note: Text baked into a bitmap blurs when enlarged, ignores high-contrast modes and user stylesheets, and is invisible to translation tools.

sources.title: Mozilla RTL guidelines
sources.note: Logical properties, and the icon-mirroring rule with its exception: mirror directional icons, never icons depicting real-world objects.

sources.title: Princeton: Dark Patterns at Scale
sources.note: 1,818 dark-pattern instances across 1,254 of 11,000 shopping sites. Countdown Timer 393/361; Activity Messages 313/264; Low-stock 632/581; Confirmshaming 169/164; Hard to Cancel 31/31. The base rates that make "the model reproduced the majority pattern" a claim rather than a guess.

sources.title: Deceptive Design: types of deceptive pattern
sources.note: Harry Brignull's taxonomy — preselection, fake urgency, fake social proof, confirmshaming, hard to cancel, hidden costs, nagging. The naming this lane's dark-pattern entries follow.

sources.title: CJEU C-673/17 (Planet49)
sources.note: Consent "is not validly constituted by way of a pre-ticked checkbox, which the user must deselect to refuse consent." Decided 1 October 2019.

sources.title: CPPA enforcement advisory: symmetry in choice
sources.note: The privacy-protective path may not be "longer, more difficult, or time-consuming" than the permissive one — the US counterpart to the EDPB's reject-all position.

sources.title: Baymard: reduce cart abandonment
sources.note: 39% abandon over extra charges; 24–26% over forced account creation. The measured cost of the two commerce defects in this lane.

sources.title: Baymard: spec sheet scannability
sources.note: 50% of sites get spec sheets wrong; multi-column spec sheets are misread as comparison sheets, "rendering the data included almost useless."

sources.title: Litmus: rendering differences in Microsoft Outlook clients
sources.note: The Word engine's actual limits: margin and padding dropped on images and divs, no height, no min/max-width, no padding on p or div. Why email HTML is a separate dialect.

sources.title: Litmus: the ultimate guide to preview text support
sources.note: What leaks into the inbox preview when no preheader is set, per client.

sources.title: Mailgun: Yahoo and Gmail bulk sender requirements
sources.note: From June 2024 bulk senders must support one-click unsubscribe with List-Unsubscribe-Post, processed within two days, plus a visible in-body link. Deliverability, not only law.

sources.title: Email on Acid: dark mode for email
sources.note: Partial versus full inversion by client, and which overrides actually hold.

sources.title: Manuel Matuzovic: I totally forgot about print style sheets
sources.note: "Printed links are completely useless if you don't know where they are leading", plus the a[href^="http"]::after technique and real examples of order pages that are unusable when printed.

sources.title: Smashing Magazine: a guide to the state of print stylesheets
sources.note: Rachel Andrew on browser printing and @page — the reference for the twelve-line block that fixes most of it.

sources.title: Adobe: PDF accessibility overview
sources.note: "A document that consists of scanned images of text is inherently inaccessible" — assistive technology cannot read or extract the words. The basis for treating a screenshot invoice as a defect, not a style choice.

sources.title: Diátaxis
sources.note: Documentation organised around what readers need rather than around the source tree; and the counterweight for api-reference-restates-the-type, since reference is MEANT to be terse.

sources.title: Docusaurus 2.0 announcement
sources.note: "Notice that the sample sites above use different colors, but still look quite the same" — the maintainers' own statement of the scaffold-sameness problem.

sources.title: Aftermath: how an SEO network built author bylines that do not exist
sources.note: The method this lane's image-filename check comes from, used in real reporting: one author photo's filename contained "cropped-Gemini_Generated_Image", another "ChatGPT-Image-Oct-20-2025", alongside claimed Oxford degrees the university confirmed never existed.

sources.title: Finsweet Client-First documentation
sources.note: The class system whose presence is evidence AGAINST generation — a human naming convention no generator produces.

sources.title: Framer: how to optimize PageSpeed Insights
sources.note: "PageSpeed Insights score is very approximate… scores vary significantly between tests, sometimes by up to 15 points." The reason this catalog reports bytes and file counts, which are deterministic, rather than a performance score.

sources.title: CVE-2025-48757: missing row-level security in generated Supabase backends
sources.note: 170 of 1,645 apps scanned from one builder's own showcase (10.3%) had critical RLS failures exposing names, addresses, phone numbers and financial records.

sources.title: Symbiotic Security: we scanned 1,072 vibe-coded apps
sources.note: 98% had security issues and 16% critical — the base rate behind testing the anon surface rather than assuming it.

sources.title: Publishing and sharing Claude artifacts
sources.note: The per-artifact isolated origin and URL shapes, for identifying a chat output being used as a product's permanent home.

sources.title: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10
sources.note: 71.6% navigate a lengthy page by headings as their primary method, against 3.7% for landmarks. The reason heading structure outranks almost everything else in this lane.

sources.title: Overlay Fact Sheet
sources.note: The vendor list, the technical limits, the privacy analysis and the signatory pledge to remediate at the source. Also the coverage claim from the community's side: "There are 0 automated tools that can detect accessibility problems accurately at anything above 30% of the time."

sources.title: ARIA Authoring Practices: read me first
sources.note: "A role is a promise" — ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviour, and breaking the promise is like a Place Order button that empties the cart. Also the canonical aria-label cloaking example.

sources.title: ARIA Authoring Practices: modal dialog pattern
sources.note: Focus moves into the dialog on open, returns to the invoking element on close, and windows under a modal are inert. The three rules four entries in this lane test.

sources.title: Using ARIA: the five rules
sources.note: The First Rule — prefer the native element — which redundant-role-on-a-semantic-element is the direct violation of; and the Fourth, on never hiding a focusable element.

sources.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
sources.note: SC 2.4.11, which names sticky headers, sticky footers and cookie banners explicitly. New enough that almost nothing implements it and no automated engine measures it.

sources.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2: Dragging Movements
sources.note: SC 2.5.7, and the trap worth restating: keyboard access does not satisfy it. The criterion is about pointer users who can click but cannot drag.

sources.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2: Label in Name
sources.note: SC 2.5.3. A mismatched accessible name breaks speech input and "may function as a hidden command that can be accidentally activated by speech-input users".

sources.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2: Reflow
sources.note: SC 1.4.10 and the 320 CSS px equivalence: 1280px at 400% zoom. The width generated responsive CSS does not reach, because it sits below the smallest named framework breakpoint.

sources.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2: Text Spacing
sources.note: SC 1.4.12, the four override values, and the failure modes they expose: vertical cutoff, horizontal truncation, and text overlapping other content.

sources.title: Sarah Higley: escaping 101
sources.note: The definitive treatment of Escape-key layering, opening with the exact failure this lane records: pressing Escape to collapse a select and closing the expense form containing it.

sources.title: Sara Soueidan: accessible notifications with ARIA live regions
sources.note: Why a toast with a button is the wrong shape: a live region is announced as one flat string, focus does not move there, and there is no mechanism to navigate to it.

sources.title: Manuel Matuzović: aria-label on generic elements
sources.note: The tested matrix showing what screen readers actually do with a labelled div — three different outcomes, none useful — and the full name-prohibited role list.

sources.title: Deque: accessible forms, the problem with placeholders
sources.note: "People with cognitive disabilities tend to have issues understanding placeholder text because they think it is pre-populated text."

sources.title: Google technical writing: error messages
sources.note: The whole anatomy in two questions — what went wrong, and how does the user fix it. Bad messages are "unactionable, vague, imprecise, confusing, inaccurate, unclear cause, unknown next steps". Also the strongest single construction in the sample: quote the user's value back beside the requirement, which makes the mismatch visible rather than asserted.

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: error message component
sources.note: "Describe what has happened and tell them how to fix it." Bans "forbidden", "illegal", "you forgot", "prohibited", and the words "valid" and "invalid"; bans "please" because it implies choice, and "sorry" because it does not help fix problems. The instruction/description split for empty fields versus constraint violations.

sources.title: NN/g: error message guidelines
sources.note: Human-readable language over technical jargon and error codes; "offer constructive solutions, not just problem statements"; and the argument against humour in failure.

sources.title: Microsoft writing style guide
sources.note: "Even when things break, don't blame the user for any problems. Your app should take responsibility instead." Also the endorsement of "we" for the company, which is why this lane flags first-person SINGULAR rather than all first person.

sources.title: Butterick's Practical Typography: line spacing
sources.note: "For most text, the optimal line spacing is between 120% and 145% of the point size" — and the ordering rule this lane's apostrophe check depends on: fix quotes first, then apostrophes.

sources.title: Richard Rutter: The Elements of Typographic Style Applied to the Web
sources.note: Leading as a function of typeface, text AND measure, and the case for unitless line-height: it ensures proportional spacing as text size changes, where a length inherits as a length.

sources.title: Pimp my Type: the ideal line length and line height
sources.note: Body around 1.5–1.6, headings around 1.1, and the rule this lane turns into a rendered check: longer lines need more line height, shorter lines need less. "Always test headings with line breaks."

sources.title: MDN: line-height
sources.note: Why unitless and length values inherit differently — the mechanism behind the fixed-units finding.

sources.title: Web Almanac 2025: page weight
sources.note: The medians this lane's budget is built from: 911 KB of images on mobile, 632 KB of JavaScript of which a median 251 KB is NEVER EXECUTED, a 2,559 KB median mobile page and an 8,337 KB p90.

sources.title: Web Almanac 2025: performance
sources.note: The LCP element is an image on 85.3% of desktop and 76% of mobile pages, which is why the image entries in this lane carry the weight they do. Only 13–15% of pages pass the render-blocking audit.

sources.title: Web Almanac 2025: generative AI
sources.note: The one published measurement of the AI palette spreading across the open web: Tailwind indigo-500 from 0.03% of all sites in Q3 2022 to 0.54% in Q4 2025. It explicitly does NOT measure page weight for AI-built pages — which is why this catalog says the population-level weight claim is unmeasured.

sources.title: Alex Russell: the performance inequality gap, 2026
sources.note: The P75 device and network this lane's budget is calculated against, and the framing that total page weight is an inequality gap rather than a performance problem: the visitor on a mid-range Android experiences a different website from the one in the design review.

sources.title: web.dev: Vodafone case study
sources.note: An A/B test rather than a correlation: a 31% LCP improvement measured against 8% more sales. The two changes named first are moving rendering to the server and resizing the hero image.

sources.title: V8: the cost of JavaScript in 2019
sources.note: Parse and compile are no longer the dominant cost — download and execution are. The source that retires the per-KB parse-time constant this lane lists as folklore.

sources.title: Calibre: the downsides of the Lighthouse performance score
sources.note: 43% of pages scoring 90+ in Lighthouse failed one or more Core Web Vitals thresholds in the field, and the score has no direct influence on search ranking.

sources.title: Nielsen Norman Group: Scrolljacking 101
sources.note: Usability testing found most participants at least mildly disoriented by scrolljacking, several reading the altered scroll behaviour as a bug rather than a design, and task-focused users dropping off.

sources.title: A Usability and Universal Design Investigation into Scrolljacking for Web Pages
sources.note: Peer-reviewed treatment of scrolljacking against user control, discoverability and assistive-technology compatibility.

sources.title: Agrawal et al., Disorders of balance and vestibular function in US adults (NHANES 2001-2004)
sources.note: 35.4% of US adults aged 40 and over had vestibular dysfunction, about 69 million people. The base rate behind prefers-reduced-motion, and the reason parallax is not a taste question.

sources.title: W3C: Understanding SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
sources.note: Names parallax scrolling directly as often non-essential animation, and vestibular reactions including dizziness, nausea and headaches.

sources.title: web.dev: prefers-reduced-motion, sometimes less movement is more
sources.note: Why parallax specifically triggers vestibular reactions: background and foreground moving at different rates.

sources.title: CSS-Tricks: Solving Sticky Hover States with @media (hover: hover)
sources.note: The hover state latches on tap on touchscreens. Also records the limit: a device with both touch and pointer answers yes to the query regardless of which the user is using.

sources.title: Adam Silver: The problem with disabled buttons and what to do instead
sources.note: Fixing one of several errors leaves the button disabled, so the interface reads as broken. Also rejects validate-as-you-type as the remedy.

sources.title: Bogdan Cerovac: When a disabled submit button becomes a dead end
sources.note: Names AI-generated code as a source of the pattern, and identifies the password-manager failure: a generated password fill does not trigger keyup, so the form is visibly complete and the button stays dead. Raises WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8.

sources.title: WebAIM discussion: whether or not to disable form submit button
sources.note: Practitioner thread. A disabled button may remain focusable and exposed to assistive technology, and disabling submission prevents users from finding their error quickly.

sources.title: W3C: Understanding SC 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose
sources.note: Level AA. Fields collecting information about the user must have their purpose programmatically identified, which in HTML means the fixed autocomplete token list.

sources.title: Orange digital accessibility guidelines: the HTML autocomplete attribute
sources.note: Practical token guide; records Google's reported figure of up to ~30% reduction in checkout time with correct autocomplete.

sources.title: CSS-Tricks: Finger-friendly numerical inputs with inputmode
sources.note: inputmode overrides the keyboard independently of the input type, which is what lets an identifier stay type=text and still open a numeric keypad.

sources.title: Stack Overflow blog: Why the number input is the worst input
sources.note: type=number is specified for values you would do arithmetic on; for identifiers it drops leading zeros, rejects typed separators and changes value on scroll.

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Error summary
sources.note: Show an error summary at the top of the page AND an in-line message at each field; the summary links to the field and takes focus. Built for people completing services under stress.

sources.title: Baymard Institute: checkout flow and form field count
sources.note: 18% of users abandoned a purchase because checkout was too long or complicated, against a tracked average cart abandonment rate of about 70%.

sources.title: Unslop UI: AI design tells ranked from a ~3.2M-post Reddit analysis
sources.note: Ranks named tells by share of comments across 47 subreddits. Treat as a measure of what people COMPLAIN about, not of what predicts generation -- but its negative results are useful: mesh/blob/aurora backgrounds and bento grids come in at ~0.1% and it advises against chasing them.

sources.title: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews (Liang et al.)
sources.note: 6.5%-16.9% of peer-review text substantially modified by an LLM; 10.6% of ICLR 2024 review sentences, 16.9% EMNLP, no significant evidence in Nature portfolio. 'meticulous' 34.7x, 'intricate' 11.2x, 'commendable' 9.8x increase in per-sentence probability at ICLR 2024. Estimated usage higher in reviews filed within 3 days of deadline, with lower self-reported confidence, and from reviewers who never reply to rebuttals; reviews containing scholarly citations are less likely to be AI-modified; higher estimated modification correlates with embedding-space homogenisation.

sources.title: Academ-AI: documenting the undisclosed use of generative artificial intelligence in academic publishing (Glynn)
sources.note: 768 published documents (633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, 28 book chapters). Prevalence of residue features: first person singular 401 (52.2%), knowledge update/cutoff 337 (43.9%), 'certainly, here' 258 (33.6%), 'important/crucial/essential to note' or 'please note' 107 (13.9%), second person 87 (11.3%), 'can/cannot provide' 76 (9.9%), 'Regenerate response' 7.9%, lack of access 54 (7.0%), self-identification as AI 52 (6.8%), 'the user' 34 (4.4%), apologetic language 6 (0.8%). About 1 in 4 cases evaded a major publisher with an explicit policy; fewer than 1 in 20 corrected post-publication. Two corrigenda claim a declaration was added while 'Regenerate response' and 'Certainly, here are' remain in the live text. 68% of articles were in journals with publication charges; represented journals had higher APCs and higher SJR metrics than peers.

sources.title: Compound Deception in Elite Peer Review: A Failure Mode Taxonomy of 100 Fabricated Citations at NeurIPS 2025 (Ansari), using GPTZero's scan
sources.note: GPTZero scanned 4,841 of 5,290 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers and verified 100 hallucinated citations across 53 papers (about 1%). Primary failure modes: Total Fabrication 66%, Partial Attribute Corruption 27%, Identifier Hijacking 4%, Placeholder Hallucination 2%, Semantic Hallucination 1%. All 100 were compound; secondary characteristics were Semantic Hallucination 63% and Identifier Hijacking 29%. 92% of contaminated papers held 1-2 fabrications, 8% held 4-13. Placeholder examples in print: 'Firstname Lastname and Others', 'URL or arXiv ID to be updated'.

sources.title: One in 277 PubMed-indexed papers in 2026 shows fabricated references, says analysis (Retraction Watch, on Topaz et al.)
sources.note: 97.1 million references verified across roughly 2.5 million PubMed-indexed papers; 4,406 fabricated references in 2,810 papers. Rate of papers with at least one fabricated reference: 1 in 2,828 (2023), 1 in 458 (2025), 1 in 277 (first seven weeks of 2026); 4 per 10,000 rising to 56.9 per 10,000. Review articles 57% higher than other types (16.7 vs 10.6 per 10,000). 91% of affected papers had only one or two. Over 98% saw no publisher action. Authors caveat that only resolvable references were examined.

sources.title: Hallucinations in Bibliographic Recommendation: Citation Frequency as a Proxy for Training Data Redundancy (Niimi)
sources.note: 100 GPT-4.1-generated bibliographic records across 20 CS topics, manually verified. Correlation between log(citation count) and factual fidelity r = 0.75, p < .001; saturation near verbatim recall above about 1,000 citations; inflection from generalisation to memorisation near 100 citations. Median split at 818 citations: factual score 1.245 (high) vs 0.725 (low), t(98) = -5.12, p < .001. Partially hallucinated records tend to keep first author, year and title while inventing journal, volume and pages.

sources.title: When AI Writes, Who Gets Cited? Evidence of Citation Monoculture Across Language Models
sources.note: Eleven models from three vendors and eight domain experts choosing at most 10 citations from blinded panels of 30, over 120 papers. Models: top-decile share 23.3-30.2% against a matched null of 15.6%; 2 to 20 of 120 papers never cited. Pooled experts sit at the null (18.9% vs 18.7% expected; 2 uncited vs 1.6 expected; p = 0.42). Mean cross-model map correlation 0.65 (0.71 noise-corrected), one principal component carrying 68-73% of cross-model variance; within-vendor 0.77-0.83 barely exceeds cross-vendor 0.63-0.70. Split-half reliability 0.86-0.95 per model against 0.03 for pooled humans. Human-model bibliography overlap at chance (2.96-3.25 vs 3.06 expected) while models overlap each other at twice chance. Uniform mixing of all eleven removes only 28% of the excess.

sources.title: Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for Autonomous Research (Beel, Kan, Baumgart)
sources.note: Seven fully generated manuscripts. Median 5 references per paper (range 2-9); only 5 of 34 total references (14.7%) from 2020 or later, with foundational textbooks cited in place of current work. 4 of 7 (57%) had missing or misplaced figures, incomplete sections including a literal 'Conclusions Here' placeholder, or duplicates; 4 of 7 (57%) contained incorrect or hallucinated numerical results. Results sections carried no confidence intervals or p-values. 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed on coding errors. Related work was 'particularly poor in all manuscripts, often with irrelevant citations', and the system failed to cite existing papers using its own exact terminology. Reviewer agent rejected 9 of 10 human papers including 4 that had been accepted. About $6 per manuscript.

sources.title: Explosion of formulaic research articles, including inappropriate study designs and false discoveries, based on the NHANES US national health database (Suchak, Aliu, Harrison, Zwiggelaar, Geifman, Spick), PLOS Biology
sources.note: Single-factor NHANES association papers: average 4 per year 2014-2021, then 33 in 2022, 82 in 2023, 190 by 9 October 2024. 169 predictor variables investigated as standalone associations with multifactorial conditions. Median analysed window 4 years (two biennial cycles), most commonly 2007-2018. Of 28 studies reporting significant associations with depression, only 13 survived False Discovery Rate correction.

sources.title: The 'Problematic Paper Screener' / Problematic Paper Screener: Trawling for fraud in the scientific literature (Cabanac, Labbe, Magazinov)
sources.note: Screens about 130 million publications weekly with nine detectors. Tortured phrases: nearly 19,000 articles with at least five each ('Joined Together States', 'bosom peril', 'Kidney disappointment', 'Fake neural organizations', 'Lactose bigotry'); around 2,900 retracted. SCIgen gibberish: over 280 papers. Feet of Clay (retracted references): more than 764,000 articles citing retracted work, about 5,000 with at least five. ChatGPT fingerprints: over 70 papers with 'Regenerate Response' or 'As an AI language model, I cannot'. The tool has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions.

sources.title: Tortured phrases: A dubious writing style emerging in science (Cabanac, Labbe, Magazinov)
sources.note: Origin of the tortured-phrase concept and the canonical example 'counterfeit consciousness' for 'artificial intelligence'. The mechanism is word-level machine paraphrasing (SpinBot and similar) used to evade text-matching plagiarism detection, not LLM generation.

sources.title: 'Positive review only': Researchers hide AI prompts in papers (Nikkei Asia, 1 July 2025) and Hidden Prompts in Manuscripts Exploit AI-Assisted Peer Review
sources.note: 17 arXiv preprints from 14 institutions across eight countries (Waseda, KAIST, Peking University, NUS, Columbia, University of Washington among them) carried hidden instructions in white or microscopic text, such as 'GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY'; targeted searches later found 18. Four categories of injected prompt, from blunt commands to evaluation frameworks instructing praise for 'impactful contributions, methodological rigor, and exceptional novelty'.

sources.title: Pangram Predicts 21% of ICLR Reviews are AI-Generated
sources.note: About 70,000-76,000 ICLR 2026 reviews analysed; 21% classified fully AI-generated and over 50% showing some AI involvement. Listed tells: bolded 2-3 word headers followed by a colon; 'shallow nit-picks rather than genuine analysis' such as requesting extra ablations or larger test sets; 'saying a lot of words that say very little'; hallucinated citations; generic praise disconnected from the paper's contributions; fabricated criticisms of methods the paper never used. Claimed false-positive rates of 1 in 10,000 general, 1 in 100,000 on held-out arXiv papers. Caveat: Pangram sells AI detection. Of author-flagged reviews, 50 of 58 (86.2%) were independently flagged fully AI-generated and 2 (3.4%) fully human.

sources.title: CoCoNUTS: Concentrating on Content while Neglecting Uninformative Textual Styles for AI-Generated Peer Review Detection (Chen et al.)
sources.note: 315,535-instance peer-review corpus over six human-AI collaboration modes. Human-written reviews average about 431 words, Mix 506, AI 494, purely machine-generated 520; machine polishing and translation shorten text (469 to 404 and 420). Pre-ChatGPT ICLR 2023 baseline gave their detector a false-positive rate below 1% for any AI involvement. Argues that style-based detectors unfairly flag permissible language polishing while missing humanised generated content, and that LLM-as-judge detectors decide on 'natural flow' and 'technical language' rather than substance.

sources.title: Does ChatGPT Ignore Article Retractions and Other Reliability Concerns? (Thelwall), Learned Publishing
sources.note: 217 papers retracted or flagged in the Retraction Watch Database, assessed 30 times each by GPT-4o-mini: 6,510 reports, none of which mentioned the retraction or validity concern, while 190 of the 217 were described as world leading, internationally excellent or close to it.

sources.title: arXiv changes rules after a flood of AI-generated survey and position papers (404 Media; arXiv CS moderation announcement, 31 October 2025)
sources.note: arXiv's computer science section now requires documented successful peer review for literature surveys and position papers, after receiving hundreds of submissions per month that moderators describe as 'little more than annotated bibliographies'. September 2025 was a record month at about 26,000 submissions. Criticism noted: the policy may disproportionately affect early-career researchers, who write a disproportionate share of review and position papers.

sources.title: Policies on artificial intelligence chatbots among academic publishers: a cross-sectional audit
sources.note: 162 STM publishers audited as of December 2023. 56 (34.6%) had a publicly available AI-chatbot policy for authors; of those 51 (91.1%) prohibited AI authorship and 46 (82.1%) required disclosure, most often in Methods or Acknowledgements. Policies for peer reviewers were explicitly out of scope.

sources.title: Apply Responsibly: Policy on AI Use in NIH Research Applications and Limiting Submissions per PI (NIH, July 2025)
sources.note: From 25 September 2025 NIH accepts six applications per PI per calendar year and will not consider applications substantially developed by AI. NIH cited PIs submitting more than 40 distinct applications in a single round; in 2024 only 1.3% of applicants submitted more than six. AI use resulting in plagiarism or fabricated citations may be referred to the Office of Research Integrity.

sources.title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: A Reproducibility Crisis
sources.note: 640 LLM-for-SE papers, 2020-2025, manually coded. Versioning smells in 32.2% (unpinned dependencies, 'latest model release'); access and legal 35.9%; code and execution 35.5%; environment and tooling 21.1%; model smells 9.2%. 199 papers gave no prompt templates, 88 documented no inference parameters, 572 mentioned no hardware, only 33 shipped Docker. Only 13.3% had no reproducibility smell at all.

sources.title: Randomness in large language models: What researchers need to know (and report)
sources.note: Supports the methods item: temperature zero removes deliberate sampling but not variation from silent model updates, numerical rounding or expert routing, so a hosted-model result without a pinned snapshot and access window is not reproducible even by its authors.

sources.title: Comparing scientific abstracts generated by ChatGPT to original abstracts (Gao et al., npj Digital Medicine)
sources.note: Generated abstracts scored 100% originality on a plagiarism detector, so text-matching tools give no signal at all. Blinded human reviewers correctly identified 68% of generated abstracts and wrongly flagged 14% of genuine ones.

sources.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of quotation inaccuracy in medicine
sources.note: Baseline for the human rate of the 'reference does not support the sentence' failure: 16.9% of quotations incorrect (95% CI 14.1%-20.0%), about half of them major (8.0%, 95% CI 6.4%-10.0%). Citation-error studies in individual specialties report 10%-37% of references with errors.

sources.title: The Prevalence of Misreporting and Misinterpreting Correlation Coefficients in Biomedical Literature
sources.note: Baseline that forecloses a tempting claim: across 310 articles in Science, Nature and Nature Neuroscience in 2022, 58.71% did not explicitly report sample sizes and 98.06% gave no confidence intervals for correlations. A p-value without an effect size or interval is the human norm, not an AI tell.

sources.title: Evaluation of spin in abstracts (psychiatry and psychology; allergy and immunology; sleep medicine; orthopaedics)
sources.note: Human base rates for abstract conclusions overstating results: 49.1% of abstract conclusion sections in psychiatry and psychology, 85.7% in allergy and immunology RCTs with nonsignificant outcomes, 71.9% in sleep medicine, 44.8% of orthopaedic RCTs with nonsignificant primary endpoints. Abstract overstatement cannot be used as an AI signal.

sources.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers (Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, Zou)
sources.note: The fairness constraint on this whole lane: seven commercial detectors averaged a 61.3% false-positive rate on TOEFL essays by non-native English writers, with 19% flagged unanimously; prompting GPT-4 to improve the word choice dropped misclassification to 11.6%, showing the detectors measure fluency rather than provenance.

sources.title: Hindawi reveals process for retracting more than 8,000 paper mill articles (Retraction Watch)
sources.note: Context for the paper-mill items: Hindawi (Wiley) retracted over 8,000 special-issue articles in 2023, more than all publishers combined had ever retracted in a single year; Wiley put the cost at $35-40 million in lost 2023 revenue and closed the brand.

sources.title: GPT-fabricated scientific papers on Google Scholar (Haider, Rodl, Soderberg, Ekstrom), Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review
sources.note: 227 questionable papers found on Google Scholar: 88 with legitimate or declared GPT use, 139 with undeclared or fraudulent use. Concentrated in applied, disinformation-susceptible topics - environment, health and computing.

sources.title: Retraction: Cellular functions of spermatogonial stem cells in relation to JAK/STAT signaling pathway (Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology)
sources.note: The retraction notice itself: 'Following publication, concerns were raised regarding the nature of its AI-generated figures'; the article 'does not meet the standards of editorial and scientific rigor'. Published 13 Feb 2024, retracted 16 Feb 2024 - three days.

sources.title: The rat with the big balls and the enormous penis - Science Integrity Digest (Elisabeth Bik)
sources.note: Primary contemporaneous account. Guo et al., Frontiers Cell Dev Biol. Midjourney disclosed by the authors. Figure labels included 'testtomcels', 'dissilced', 'iollotte sserotgomar', 'sterrn cells'. Supports generated-anatomical-or-mechanism-schematic.

sources.title: Study Featuring AI-Generated Giant Rat Penis Retracted, Journal Apologizes (Vice)
sources.note: Frontiers' own statement: 'one of the reviewers raised valid concerns about the figures and requested author revisions. The authors failed to respond to these requests.' Corrects the common claim that no reviewer looked - one did, and the process failed to act.

sources.title: Giant rat penis redux: AI-generated diagram, errors lead to retraction (Retraction Watch)
sources.note: Second incident: Lippincott's Medicine, retracted 12 July 2024. Figure 4 had the wrong number of bones in the lower leg and arm and labels reading 'chlsinkestead atlvs no ctivktty greuedis'; corresponding author admitted using ChatGPT.

sources.title: Bik EM, Casadevall A, Fang FC. The Prevalence of Inappropriate Image Duplication in Biomedical Research Publications. mBio 7(3), 2016
sources.note: The prevalence figure and its methodology: manual visual screening of 20,621 papers from 40 journals, 1995-2014; 3.8% contained problematic figures; at least half showed features suggestive of deliberate manipulation. Predates generative models entirely.

sources.title: Weissgerber TL, Milic NM, Winham SJ, Garovic VD. Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm. PLOS Biology 13(4):e1002128, 2015
sources.note: 703 original articles, top 25% of physiology journals, Jan-Mar 2014: 85.6% included at least one bar graph, 77.6% of those mean with SE; univariate scatterplots 13.4%, box plots 5.3%, histograms 8.0%. Median minimum n per group = 3. Recommends univariate scatterplots, box plots and histograms.

sources.title: Crameri F, Shephard GE, Heron PJ. The misuse of colour in science communication. Nature Communications 11:5444, 2020
sources.note: Colour-driven misinterpretation 'can diverge from an objective representation by more than seven percent of the displayed data variation'. CVD prevalence quoted as 8% of men, 0.5% of women worldwide. Lists the properties of a scientific colour map and states that including the colour bar is imperative.

sources.title: Borland D, Taylor MR. Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful. IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications 27(2), 2007
sources.note: The canonical anti-rainbow argument: perceptual non-uniformity confuses the viewer, obscures data and actively misleads interpretation.

sources.title: Ware C, Stone M, Szafir DA. Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad. IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications 43(3):88-93, 2023
sources.note: The honest counterpoint used in rainbow-or-jet-colormap's false_positive_when: rainbow maps have underappreciated advantages, particularly for reading precise values and surfacing fine structure. The consensus is not unanimous.

sources.title: matplotlib default matplotlibrc (main branch)
sources.note: Read directly for the exact defaults used across this lane: figure.figsize 6.4, 4.8; figure.dpi 100; savefig.dpi 'figure'; savefig.format png; font.size 10.0; font.sans-serif starts DejaVu Sans; axes.prop_cycle cycler(color='tab10'); image.cmap viridis; legend.loc best; axes.formatter.useoffset True; axes.formatter.limits -5, 6; figure.constrained_layout.use False; axes.grid False.

sources.title: Nature research figure guide: building and exporting figure panels
sources.note: Column widths 89 mm single and 183 mm double, maximum height 170 mm; minimum text size 5 pt, maximum 7 pt; Arial or Helvetica; vector (.ai, .eps, .pdf) preferred for main figures with .jpeg/.tiff/.png rejected; 'do not outline text'. Used for figsize-not-matched-to-the-column-width and line-chart-shipped-as-a-raster.

sources.title: PLOS figure requirements
sources.note: TIFF or EPS only; width minimum 789 px and maximum 2250 px at 300 dpi; height maximum 2625 px; resolution 300-600 dpi; 'use only Arial, Times, or Symbol font in 8-12 point'. The 789 px minimum is what a default 640 px matplotlib PNG fails outright.

sources.title: Elsevier artwork overview
sources.note: 300 dpi for halftone, 1000 dpi for line art, 500 dpi for combination art. Used in savefig-at-the-default-dpi.

sources.title: Cumming G, Fidler F, Vaux DL. Error bars in experimental biology. Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11, 2007
sources.note: The canonical statement that SD, SE and CI bars give different information and that figure legends must say which is shown; SD does not change with n while SE and CI shrink. Underpins error-bars-of-undeclared-type.

sources.title: Wullschleger et al. High Incorrect Use of the Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) in Original Articles in Three Cardiovascular Journals Evaluated for 2012. PLOS ONE 9(10):e110364
sources.note: 441 original articles from 2012 across three cardiovascular journals: 64% contained at least one incorrect use of SEM (per journal 72%, 73%, 27%); in 81% of those the authors had explicitly stated in the Methods that they used SEM for data description.

sources.title: Wasserstein RL, Lazar NA. The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician 70(2):129-133, 2016
sources.note: 'Practices that reduce data analysis or scientific inference to mechanical bright-line rules (such as p < 0.05) ... can lead to erroneous beliefs and poor decision making', and the variants should not survive 'whether expressed in words, by asterisks in a table, or in some other way'. Used in significance-stars-with-no-test-named.

sources.title: Pandey AV, Rall K, Satterthwaite ML, Nov O, Bertini E. How Deceptive are Deceptive Visualizations? CHI 2015
sources.note: Measured distortion effects including truncated axis: participants shown deceptive visualisations reported interpretations 58.5% to 129.5% larger than controls; in message-reversal conditions 97.5% of the deceptive group answered in the wrong direction.

sources.title: Correll M, Bertini E, Franconeri S. Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace? CHI 2020
sources.note: Cited for the false_positive_when on truncated-or-dual-axis-without-a-declaration: the anti-truncation position is contested, and a blanket ban is not supported.

sources.title: Cleveland WS, McGill R. Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods. JASA 79(387):531-554, 1984
sources.note: The accuracy ordering of elementary perceptual tasks: position along a common scale most accurate, then length, then angle and slope, then area. The reason a pie asks the reader for the two worst judgements.

sources.title: Siegrist M. The use or misuse of three-dimensional graphs to represent lower-dimensional data. Behaviour & Information Technology 15(2), 1996
sources.note: Used to keep the 3D claim honest rather than to inflate it: mean pie-reading error 2.7% in 2D against 3.2% in 3D, a 0.5-point difference, plus a latency cost. Cited inside the false_positive_when.

sources.title: ggplot2 reference: scale_colour_hue (evenly spaced colours for discrete data)
sources.note: Defaults h = c(0, 360) + 15, c = 100, l = 65; the documentation itself states the scale is not colour-blind safe and that because the colours all have the same luminance and chroma they appear as an identical shade of grey in black and white.

sources.title: Identifying images in the biology literature that are problematic for people with a colour-vision deficiency. eLife 2024;13:e95524
sources.note: 66,253 eLife images downloaded (2012-2022); in the 4,964-image manually reviewed set, 636 (12.8%) were 'definitely problematic' for deuteranopes and 3,865 (77.9%) 'definitely okay'. Problematic rate declined 2012-2021 with a modest rise in 2022.

sources.title: Figure accessibility for readers with colour vision deficiency: analysis of leading medical journals (medRxiv preprint)
sources.note: 138 figure plates (395 sub-figures) from 27 research articles across 9 leading medical journals: 107 (80%) failed WCAG colour-contrast and labelling requirements; 215 of 395 sub-figures (55%) judged completely inaccessible to protan or deutan readers. Preprint - treat accordingly.

sources.title: Colour Blind Awareness: types of colour blindness
sources.note: The population figure used throughout: general agreement that worldwide about 8% of men and 0.5% of women have a red-green colour-vision deficiency. Note Crameri et al. add that rates are lower in sub-Saharan African populations and higher in northern European ones, so 'up to 8%' is the honest phrasing.

sources.title: Dong H. Self-Distillation Policy Optimization via Visual Feedback: Bridging Code and Visual Artifacts. arXiv:2606.10334 (Microsoft), June 2026
sources.note: The lane's governing mechanism, stated in the source: code-generating LLMs produce charts 'by writing programs that are executed by non-differentiable renderers, committing to code before observing the render', so valid programs yield 'visually salient defects, including overlapping elements, clipped text, broken alignment, low contrast, and overflow'. Also: 'legends overlap data, text is clipped at frame boundaries, elements collide'.

sources.title: Galimzyanov T, Titov S, Golubev Y, Bogomolov E. Drawing Pandas: A Benchmark for LLMs in Generating Plotting Code. arXiv:2412.02764
sources.note: 175 tasks. GPT-4o best at visual mean 75/100 with only 69% of plots scoring 75 or above; Plotly 22% incorrect code against Matplotlib 1.8%. Most relevant number for this lane: replacing the task with a generic 'plot a given dataframe' collapses the visual mean from 75 to 44 and the good-score ratio from 0.69 to 0.32 - unreviewed plotting, measured.

sources.title: SciFigDetect: A Benchmark for AI-Generated Scientific Figure Detection. arXiv:2604.08211
sources.note: Why this lane refuses to hand over a generated-figure detector. 72,965 real and 150,807 synthetic figures. Zero-shot: best method 53.68% average accuracy, most near the 33% chance level, with roughly 100% accuracy on real figures and 0-3% on synthetic. Cross-generator transfer collapses (train on one generator, 26.1% on the other). JPEG q=30 drops the best method from 93.96% to 75.94%; Gaussian noise sigma=20 to 50.49%.

sources.title: AI detectors are poor western blot classifiers: a study of accuracy and predictive values. PeerJ 2025
sources.note: 96 western blot images (48 ChatGPT-4-generated, 48 authentic from 2015 papers). Four-lane blots: Is It AI? accuracy 0.75 (sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.54); Hive Moderation 0.53 (sensitivity 0.19); Illuminarty 0.56. Positive predictive values 'very low at realistic probabilities'. Conclusion: free AI-detection tools should be used with great caution on western blots.

sources.title: Springer Nature AI guidance for researchers and communities
sources.note: Policy basis for generated-figure-against-the-publisher-policy: Springer Nature journals are unable to permit generative-AI images and video for publication, with narrow exceptions for contractually licensed agency art and for pieces specifically about AI, reviewed case by case. Text-based and numerical display items such as tables and simple graphs are outside the policy.

sources.title: Gabelica M, Bojcic R, Puljak L. Many researchers were not compliant with their published data sharing statement: a mixed-methods study. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 150:33-41, 2022
sources.note: Of 1,792 manuscripts whose data-availability statement said the authors were willing to share, 1,670 (93%) did not respond or declined; 254 (14%) responded and only 122 (6.8%) provided the data. Note: Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, not the BMJ, which several secondary sources get wrong.

sources.title: Nature: initial submission - figure guidelines
sources.note: Backs the reporting requirements in error-bars-of-undeclared-type and sample-size-absent-from-the-figure: error bars must be defined throughout the figures and exact n values must be given, reported individually rather than as a range where n varied.

sources.title: l2tabu: An essential guide to LaTeX2e usage -- obsolete commands and packages (English, source)
sources.note: The canonical obsolete-forms list, read in full: {\bf}/{\it}/{\rm} and the NFSS argument, $$...$$ and fleqn, \over vs \frac, \centerline, eqnarray vs align, \def vs \newcommand, center-inside-float vs \centering, a4/a4wide, epsfig/psfig, doublespace, fancyheadings, scrlettr, caption2. Dated 2003-2007, which is why the obsolete-markup item is marked fading and its false-positive line says so.

sources.title: CTAN: package nag -- detecting and warning about obsolete LaTeX commands
sources.note: \usepackage[l2tabu,orthodox]{nag} turns the l2tabu list into compile-time warnings ('Package nag Warning: Command \bf is an old LaTeX 2.09 command'). The mechanical detection path for obsolete-two-oh-nine-markup.

sources.title: ChkTeX source: FindErrs.h warning table
sources.note: The authoritative numbered warning list, extracted verbatim: W2 non-breaking space, W8 wrong dash length, W9/W10/W15/W17/W47/W48/W49 environment and brace mismatch, W16 math still on at EOF, W18 straight double quote, W29 $\times$, W34 mixed quotes, W35 operator names, W41 primitive TeX in LaTeX, W45 $$ vs \[.

sources.title: ChkTeX default configuration (chktexrc)
sources.note: Supplies the two closed lists used in this lane: Linker { \ref \vref \pageref \eqref \cite } for the tie rule, and MathRoman { log lg ln lim sin cos tan ... } for operator names.

sources.title: TeXtidote rule list
sources.note: Named rule IDs for four items here: sh:nobreak (do not break lines manually with \\), sh:hcfig/sh:hctab/sh:hcsec/sh:hccha (do not refer to figures/tables/sections by hard-coded number), sh:relpath (figures must not use hard-coded local paths), sh:figref (every figure should have a label and be referenced). Also sh:nonp, sh:capperiod, sh:nsubdiv, sh:secskip, sh:stacked, sh:c:mix, sh:c:mul.

sources.title: TeXpert: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Evaluating LaTeX Code Generation by LLMs
sources.note: The measurement this lane leans on hardest. 440 prompts, nine models. Error distribution: syntax 1.3-5.3%, package 15.2-29.9%, formatting 20.6-25.3%, logical 44.3-59.1%. Overall accuracy GPT-4o 66.1%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 55.0%, Gemini 1.5 Flash 41.8%; hard set 0-17.5%. Worked examples include \includegraphics without graphicx and \ref{sec:1} without \label{sec:1}. Authors note non-standard package use 'may point to LLMs hallucinating or making up packages'.

sources.title: TeXFix-Bench: An Empirically Grounded Multi-Format Benchmark for LLM-Based Document Source Repair
sources.note: Mined taxonomy of 168 verified localized hard-crash LaTeX faults from TeX.SE, GitHub commits and package docs. UndefinedControlSequence 18.5%, OtherFatalCompile 10.1%, InputEncoding 9.5%, BraceGroup 8.9%, MathMode 8.9%, GraphicsInclude 7.1%. Important for fairness: this is the HUMAN fault distribution, which is why the lane's claim is about whether anyone opened the PDF, not about who typed the source.

sources.title: X-raying the arXiv: A Large-Scale Analysis of arXiv Submissions' Source Files
sources.note: About 600,000 submissions, 2015-2025: 27% of uploaded bytes are not needed to produce the PDF (584GB), rising from ~14% in 2015-2017 to 32% in 2022. Qualitative pass found offensive comments about coauthors and reviewers, over 1,500 Google Docs links with at least 200 open to anyone with the link, and notes suggesting authors avoid mentioning limitations.

sources.title: arXiv FAQ: Why Submit the TeX/LaTeX Source?
sources.note: arXiv itself raises 'What if my TeX source has potentially embarrassing self-comments in it?' and points at arxiv_latex_cleaner. Establishes that the .tex is public, which is the whole basis for comment-residue-in-public-source.

sources.title: google-research/arxiv-latex-cleaner
sources.note: The mechanical fix: strips all comments (including \begin{comment} and \iffalse/\if0 blocks), named commands via --commands_to_delete, named environments, unused .tex files and unreferenced images.

sources.title: TeX StackExchange Q139873: What are the most common mistakes that beginners of (La)TeX make?
sources.note: Read via the Stack Exchange API. Highest-voted substantive answer names, in order: ending every paragraph with \\ or \\[10pt]; \bfseries{important} used as if it took an argument; carrying enormous donated preambles; \begin{table}[h!] for content that must not float; unprotected capitals in BibTeX titles; words in italic math subscripts (S_{easy}); and hand-built headings using \\[12pt]\textbf{2.3 ...}. Other answers add redundant/duplicate packages, package load-order problems, and \def redefinition accidents.

sources.title: TeX StackExchange Q173717: Is it ever bad to use \left and \right?
sources.note: David Carlisle's \mathinner argument (extra spacing, no line breaking in display or inline, rigid enclosed space) plus the TeXbook pp. 148-149 excerpt naming three cases where \left/\right pick the wrong size. Directly contradicts dspinellis/latex-advice, which is recorded in conflicts.

sources.title: dspinellis/latex-advice
sources.note: Consolidated practitioner guide. Supports: symbolic references via \Cref and self-descriptive labels; avoid \hline and | in tables, use booktabs; \centering not center inside floats; reference every float and place it before its first reference; thin non-breaking space between number and unit via siunitx; brace capitals in BibTeX titles and keep journal-name format consistent; drop URL when a DOI exists; new font commands not old switches; tie before \cite and \ref; run lacheck and chktex. Also the source of the \left/\right contradiction.

sources.title: Wookai/paper-tips-and-tricks
sources.note: Corroborates the tie rule (Figure~\ref), booktabs with no vertical rules, siunitx for all numbers and units, and $$...$$ as one of the 'deadly sins' with a direct citation to l2tabu.

sources.title: booktabs manual: Publication quality tables in LaTeX (Simon Fear)
sources.note: The exact rule, as stated: '1. Never, ever use vertical rules. 2. Never use double rules.' Primary source for vertical-rules-and-full-grid-tables.

sources.title: NIST: SI Unit rules and style conventions checklist
sources.note: Item 15: 'There is a space between the numerical value and unit symbol, even when the value is used in an adjectival sense.' Item 16: digits in groups of three separated by a thin fixed space, commas not used. Primary source for number-and-unit-run-together, including the percent/degree standards conflict.

sources.title: siunitx package documentation
sources.note: The fix side of the units item: \qty, \num, \qtyrange, the S column for decimal alignment, and one place to change the convention.

sources.title: acmart samples.dtx (ACM article template sources)
sources.note: Source of the exact placeholder literals: \acmConference[Conference acronym 'XX]{Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email}{June 03--05, 2018}{Woodstock, NY}, plus 'The Name of the Title is Hope' and the 978-1-4503-XXXX-X ISBN.

sources.title: Published and preprint papers still carrying 'Conference acronym XX / Woodstock, NY'
sources.note: Evidence the placeholder survives to publication rather than being a hypothetical: a search for the literal returns arXiv PDFs, ResearchGate uploads, a Microsoft Research CHI submission PDF and an accepted-papers list. This is why conference-template-residue is severity high.

sources.title: NeurIPS LaTeX template (Overleaf)
sources.note: Source of the 'David S.~Hippocampus' placeholder author literal.

sources.title: IEEE Conference Template (Overleaf)
sources.note: Source of the 'Given Name Surname', 'dept. name of organization (of Aff.)', 'email address or ORCID' and 'Paper Title (use style: paper title)' placeholder literals.

sources.title: ACL Rolling Review: Authors Beware -- Common Submission Problems
sources.note: Names the anonymization switch ('the template has a [review] setting that must be on for the submission'), forbids non-anonymous repository links and an acknowledgements section in a submission, requires 'the standard vertical spacing for figures, tables, title', requires 'no comments or any leftover meta-text from prior revisions', and states that submissions attempting to manipulate machine readers will be desk rejected.

sources.title: acl-org/aclpubcheck
sources.note: The PDF-side mechanical checker: font errors, author formatting, margin violations (approximately 2cm clear at the bottom of each page), page numbering, and citation checks against the ACL Anthology, DBLP and arXiv. The rendered-confirm path for negative-vspace-to-hit-page-limit and overfull-box-shipped.

sources.title: ICLR formatting instructions (\iclrfinalcopy) and CVPR author guidelines (\cvprfinalcopy)
sources.note: 'If your paper is ultimately accepted, the statement \iclrfinalcopy should be inserted to adjust the format to the camera ready requirements.' CVPR's equivalent: 'LaTeX users may uncomment the \cvprfinalcopy command in the document preamble' and the camera ready must not contain a ruler. Both are the one-line switch behind anonymization-state-mismatch.

sources.title: Nikkei: 'Positive review only' -- researchers hide AI prompts in papers
sources.note: The measurement behind hidden-instruction-to-machine-reader: 17 arXiv preprints, lead authors at 14 institutions including Waseda, KAIST, Peking University, NUS, Washington and Columbia; prompts one to three sentences long; concealed with white text or extremely small font sizes.

sources.title: Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Generated Reviews of Scientific Papers
sources.note: Academic follow-up, with the white-text-on-white-ground mechanism illustrated and the canonical injected string quoted. Used for the pdftotext-vs-visible-page detection method rather than for any rate claim.

sources.title: CTAN JSON API (package existence)
sources.note: Verified live during this research: a real package returns a JSON record, an invented one returns {"errors":["Not found"]}. Also verified its failure mode -- algpseudocode returns Not found because the .sty ships inside the algorithmicx bundle -- which is why usepackage-that-does-not-exist puts kpsewhich first and CTAN second.

sources.title: CTAN obsolete/ tree: subfigure
sources.note: 'The package is now considered obsolete: it was superseded by subfig, but users may find the more recent subcaption package more satisfactory.' Anchors the superseded-package map in kitchen-sink-preamble.

sources.title: cleveref manual and TeX.SE Q1863 on hyperref load order
sources.note: 'Basically, cleveref must be loaded last.' hyperref's own documentation: 'Make sure it comes last of your loaded packages.' Documented exceptions after cleveref: hypdvips and autonum. Primary source for hyperref-load-order-violation, including its false-positive line.

sources.title: Claus Wilke: How to not mess up your bibliographies with BibTeX
sources.note: The brace-protection rule with worked examples (title = {A review of {HIV} biology}), and the warning against double-bracing the whole title. Supports the fix side of hand-rolled-bibliography.

sources.title: TeX.SE Q1380: how to avoid the BibTeX 'repeated entry' error
sources.note: Confirms BibTeX's behavior is fatal and unavoidable ('Repeated entry---line N of file refs.bib', 'I'm skipping whatever remains of this entry'), which is what makes duplicate-bibtex-key a defect rather than a preference.

sources.title: r/LaTeX community observation on chatbot-generated LaTeX
sources.note: 'Chatgpt has a tendency to utilize outdated, unsupported packages.' Recorded as a community observation supporting kitchen-sink-preamble and obsolete-two-oh-nine-markup, NOT as a measurement -- no rate is claimed anywhere in this lane on its basis.

sources.title: USENIX ;login:: We Have a Package for You -- package hallucinations in LLM-generated code
sources.note: The mechanism behind usepackage-that-does-not-exist, established for npm and PyPI. Cited for the mechanism only: no equivalent study exists for CTAN, which is stated as a refusal.

sources.title: Overleaf documentation: 'There were undefined references' and float placement specifiers
sources.note: The compile-visible side of dangling references (?? in output, 'LaTeX Warning: Reference X on page N undefined') and the h/H/htbp placement semantics, including that [H] requires the float package and [!h] is silently changed to [!ht].
